in: El Paso. ~ 7

than at first intimated. The defense_of
Dueidar. was gallantly. maintained by

The enemy suffered severe casualties
from bombs dropped and from machine
gun fire. ;
“There was no further fighting on

Special to The New York Times.

WASHINGTON, April 25.—Henry Mor-
genthau of New York ,nas tendered to
President Wilson his resignation as Am-
bassador to Turkey. No action has Been
taken on the resignation, but it is as-
sured that the President will accept it.
Mr. Morgenthau has been credited with
an intention to leave the Diplomatic
Service, and, according to gossip here,
Abram. I. Elkus of New York will be of-
fered the Ambassadorship to Tu-key.

The purpose of Mr. Morgenthau in re-
signing is to enable him to take an ac-
tive part in the forthcoming political
campaign in behalf of President Wilson.
When he -eturned to the United States
from Constantinople last February he

close friends and supporters of the Ad-
ministration a plan for the formation of
a league in the interest of Mr. Wilson’s
re-election, this league to be composed
of ‘business men and others, and to in-
clude in its membership independents
and. persons formerly affiliated with
other political parties who were willing
to support the Democratic cause this

ear.

7 While Mr. Morgenthau was willing to
take charge of the formation of- the
league, he felt that he could not: remain
i this pit A engaged in political work
while he retained his Ambassadorial of-
fice. Men. prominent in the Adminis-
tration urged him not to resign, and
expressed the opinion that there would
be no fmpropriety in his remaining in
the Diplomatic rvice.

PRECEDENT FOR DECISION

Washington Sees Possibility of a
) Diplomatic Snarl Qver the
von Igel Documents.

Special to The New York Times.

WASHINGTON, April .—Secretary
Lansing has decided to give to Count
von Bernstorff, the German Ambassa-
dor; only those documents which the
Ambassador identifies as ‘official ”’
from among the papers taken from the
raided New York office of Wolf von
Igel of the German Embassy staff, who
was arrested by Department of Justice
agents in connection with the plot to
destroy the Welland Canal.

It ‘Was learned today that the Secre-
tary of State is determined in the stand
he has taken not to authorize the re-
turn of any of these papers until and
unless they are identified by the Am-
bassador as. being ‘' official,””. which
means that they must be claimed as
Embassy records. Officials of the Gov-
ernment will not attempt to identify
any papers as official. The identifica-
tion must be made by the Ambassador

or someone designated to represent his

Embassy. Papers not identified as of-
ficial will be held by the Government.

Should some documents be claimed as
official, such identification is expected

to prove embarrassing to the Embassy

because it would be regarded as linking

the Embassy with knowledge of illegal

activities covered by these Particular

documents,

The fact that the- Administration is
determined to make an issue over the
return of the papers is likely to pre-
cipitate a stiff diplomatic row unless
the German Ambassador should with-
draw his demand for the return of all
the von Igel papers. There had been in-
timations during the past few days that
this Government might be willing to
permit the return of all the von Igel
documents. The fact that only such doc-
uments as Count von Bernstorff may
identify as ‘‘ official’* may be claimed
indicates that the Administration has
decided to take a firm stand in the
matter.

It became evident today that this Gov-
ernment is prepared to resist Count*von
Bernstorff’s claim that all papers be-
longing to diplomatic agents are im-
mune from seizure. . ;

‘BRITISH HOUSES
IN SECRET SESSION

Curzon and Rosebery Resume
Their Seats in the Lords for
the Momentous Occasion.

GREAT PRECAUTIONS TAKEN

Even Ventilator Sealed to Pre-
vent Eavesdropping—Recruit-
ing Plan to be Made Public.

LONDON, Wednesday, April 26.—The
most crowded houses since the war be-
gan were drawn to Westminster Palace
yesterday by the excitement attending
the secret session of Parliament,

coupled with the news of various
stirring incidents. ° Earl .Curzon made
his first. appearance in the House of
Lords since his illness. The Earl of
Rosebery, who had not been seen there
since the commencement of the war,
‘also was in his seat.** The interest of
the public was shown by -the large
crowd which assembled to watch the
atrival of the Ministers and members. »

Extraordinary precautions were taken
to prevent unauthorized persons. over-
hearing the proceedings. All. the doors
leading to the House of Commons not
only were locked but secured by pad-
locks which had been specially pro-
vided, while the police searched every
nook and cranny. of the great building,
scoured the vaults and underground
cotridors, and even. sealed the grille of
the ventilator in the floor of the cham-
ber so that nothing said could by any
chance reach the éars of any one below.

Traditional customs were followed in
the House of Commons. which was open
asp usual to attachés, representatives of
the press, and spectators until the ‘end
of the question period. At that time
Premier Asquith observed the ancient
practice of taking notice that strangers
were present. The question was put
that strangers myst be ordered to with-
draw,.which does not permit of. debate
or amendment. Beforé the house was
adjourned at night it was arranged that
the sitting should be resumed today
under similar conditions,

In the House of Lords the only pro-
cedure was to give notice that no one
exvept members would be permitted in
the Chamber.

The Marquis of Crewe, Lord President
of the Council, in moving that the sitting
be in secret, made.a statement on behalf
of the Government why this course
should be adopted. Although the mem-

the Cabinet. were all set on the
pc Paar dlbewec of a victory, the Marquis
said, they did not agree concerning the
number of men or the kind sf men who
were available-for service‘in the army
and navy, nor did they agree as to the
proper means for securing those who
were available.

The course which the Government Le
posed to recommend to Parliament might
not meet with.
of either extreme views, and therefore
it was the Government's duty to récom-
mend it.as far. as possible to the opinion
of Parliament as a whole, which neéces-
sitated the making of a statement. con-
taining confidential information. Hence
the Government had decided to hold.a
secret session, ‘‘ publishing at an early
date a considered description of. ‘the
proposal which the\Government in due
course would make ‘to Parliament and

ountry.’’
thene Marquis of Lincolnshire as Lord
Great Chamberlain explained that, in
accordance with the hereditary duties
of his office, he had taken steps to see
that the secrecy would be “‘ most strict-

d solemnly coeerves He had, he
said caused a search be made “of
the whole -House, the lobbies, and the
vaults below.”’

STRIVES TO AID NEUTRALS

Government Said to be Doing All in
Its Power to Limit incon-
veniences to Trade.

WASHINGTON, April 25.—The latest
British note in answer to Amierican
protests against allied interference with
neutral trade, made public tonight at
the Staté Department, contends that the
practices complained of aré ‘ juridical-
ly’ sound and valid” and that the re-
lief which neutrals seek is rather to be
obtained by. the mitigation of necessary
hardships than by “abrupt changes
either in the theory or application of
a policy based upon admitted princi-
ples of international law carefully ad-
justed to the altered ee of mod-
ern warfare.”

It discloses that ‘‘an:impartial and
influential commission” has been ap-
pointed to find ways to minimize de-
lays, and pledges the Allies to make
their restraints on trade as little bur-
densome to neutrals as possible. The
note, in which the French Government
concurs, reiterates the military necessity
of regulating commerce to neutrals
contiguous to Germany, and justifies the
effectiveness of the blockade which was
challenged by the last American note.
More diplomatic correspondence over the
issue is expected to follow.

which, he was solemnly pledged by
treaty to protect. The disregard of neu-

to naval warfare by the wanton de-
struction of neutral merchant ehips on

Civil War Precedent.

The note refers to the action taken by
the United States during the civil war
to stop such trade, and to the Supreme
Court’s doctrine of continuous voyage,
given to cover all cases where there
was an intention to thwart the block-
ade by ‘‘ whatever means, direct’ or in-
direct.’’

“His Majesty’s Government desire to
assure the United States Government,”’
the note continues, ‘‘ that eve effort
is being made to distinguish tween

na-fide neutral commerce and hae

which really is intended for the enem
The task is one of exceptional difficulty,
and the statistics show that a at vol-
ume of imports intended y ay the enemy
must have passed through adjacent neu-

instance, the imports of “ard into Swe-
den pete the year 1915 may be taken.
year the total imports of lard

three years before the war the average
‘annual import of the same article was
only 888 tons, of which 6388 came from
the United States. It is difficult to be-
lieve that the requirements of Sweden
in respect of lard, even when every al-
lowance is made for possible diversions
of trade due to the war, could suddenly
have increaned tenfold in 1915. The in-
ference, indeed, is irresistible that the
eater part of these imports must have
od another and an enemy destination.”’

under the orders referred to, is shown
by the small number of vessels which
escape the allied patrols. It is doubt-
ful whether there ever has been a block-
ade where the ships which slipped
through bore so small a proportion to
those which were intercepted. The best

roof of a thoroughness of a blockade
8s to be found in results. The great
Tise in price in Germany of many
articles most necessary to the enemy
in the prosecution of the present war
must be well known to the United States
Government.”’

“ARRIVES IN FRANCE}

First Contingent, Which Came}
Last Week, Is Now Camped —
at Troyes. ~~

MARSEILLES, April 25.—Another con- | ~“:

tingent of Russian troops arrived here
this morning. They were received with
all military honors and debarked amid
énthusiastic cheers.

The contingent arrived at 10 o'clock in
the morning, their coming being greeted
by the flying of flags. and blowing of
whistles from’ the craft of many nations
in the harbor and by a large crowd
tnassed on the quay. A regiment of
Hussars acted as a guard of honor, and
General Minissier, the Governor of
Marseilles, accompanied by his staff,
welcomed the commander of the Rus-
sian force.

The Russian: aioe! assembled on the
decks, replied to the greeting from the
shore and harbor with hearty cheers,
and after landing marched through the
streets on their way to Camp Mirabegu
amid a tumultuous welcome from crowds
on the street, in balconies, and on house-
sone They occupy the same quarters,

did the Russians who arrived last
pen dit and are now at Camp Mailly, near
Troyes, on the Seine, ninety miles south-
east of Paris.

The Russian and French troops
mingling at this camp in a genera epirit
of good-will.

“The 900 who compose our member-

-‘* This, broadly, does no great harm

terri

Henor Memory of Knapp.

The membérs of The Associated Press,
at their morning session, adopted -eso-
lutions on the death of Charles W.

. Knapp, a Director, who resigned as
publisher of The St, Louis Republic to

become Treasurer of THE NEW YORK
Times. The resolutions follow:

The sudden and tragic death of Charles
W. Knapp, one of the most active founders
-of a co-operative system of news gathering
and for many years one of the most use-
ful, inspiring, and notably efficient mem-
bers of the Board of Directors of The As-
pee gn Press, evoked a profound sense of

Mr. app’s long and faithful activity
fin the d&@zelopment and maintenance of an
impartial and «accurate method for the col-
lection and distribution of information de-
ferves the gratitude of every citizen of the

country.

His” sterling integrity, superior intelli-
~ gence, judicid] temperament, and high pur-
Pose, in every phase of the responsibility
attached to the work of the organization.
challenged the admiration and affection of

his associates.

The Associated Press has suffered an ir-
reéparable ‘oss, We deeply mourn his taking
off and tender his Pereaved family our
sincere sympathy. ,

Following the adoption of the reselu-
tions, Victor F. Lawson, publisher of
The Chicago Daily News, eulogized Mr.

** He was conservative in judgment and
opinion, but open to the light of new

main his debtor for the years of able
and faithful service which he devoted to
the organization. and establishment of

e Associated Press.

“A review of the earlier years of the
absociation reminds how large and con-

atructiye work of that period of basic

evelopment, and how many of those

verning principles of The Associated

ess, ich the course of the years has
stalliized into the axioms of its ad
ministration, were suggested and formu-
lated by his judicial mind. ~The history
- of The Associated Press is in no small

Dr. Armstrong Tells the Cost of
Wage Earners’ Iliness.

Iridustrial preparedness was empha-
sized yesterday at the Health Depart-
ment in a talk before the staff of the
Bureau of Communicable Diseases by
Dr. Donald B. Armstrong, Director of
the Department of Social Welfare of
the New York Association for Improv-
ing the Condition of the Poor. ° Dr.

Armstrong pointed out the tremendous
waste that occurred annually in indus-
try as a result of unnecessary sickness
and accident.’ He said the 33,000,000 in-
dustrial workers in the United States
lost about 284,000,000 working days each
year as a result of sickn alone. This
meant financial loss, including wages,
loss to industry, and medical cost, of
nearly $500,000,000, a very serious symp-
tom of industrial preparedness and
inefficiency, the sapfeaker said, in view
of the fact that at least one-half of
this sickness was from strictly prevent-
able causes.

_Of the relation of industrial effi-
sancy. to national safety Dr. Armstrong
said:

‘‘ The European war has demonstrated
that a large army and navy are effec-
tive only if backed by an efficient in-
dustrial. organization. As a matter of
fact, the war is largely a struggle be-

cratic inefficiency. The great problem
which the United States shares in com-
mon with other democracies is that of
making democracy efficient. Any pro-
gram for preparedness which leaves
‘out of account unnecessary industrial
wastage is futile and infantile, if it is
not selfish and prejudiced.”

GET THREAD FROM LUPINE.

Germany Finds New Use for a Com-
mon Plant.

BERLIN, April 5, (Correspondence of
The Associated Press.)—Thread and fila-
ment of a practical, usable kind can
be made from the stalks of the common,
and in Germany very plentiful, lupine, a
legume belonging to the alfalfa family.
Two men who made the discovery and a
Captain who has perfected a machine
for.the process have taken out patents,
and the Prussian Ministry of Agricult-

@e has issued an appeal to farmers to
plant as much lupine as possible this

e discovery is especially welcome at
this time, when thread is scarce. Ex-
periments have proved that the best
thread from the lupine comes from the
mature ,plant, which means that lupine
culture will not have to be checked, at
the expénse of the seed, in.order to ob-
tain thread. Nor does thrashing injure
the thread part of the stalk in the least.
Captain von Bluecher’s machine, just
invented, can be moved ‘from farm to
farm, much as a thrashing machine is
moved, so that the lupine can be handled
without any transportation difficulties.
The two kinds of lupine prevailing in
Germany will grow in almost any fina
of soil, but especially in sandy, dry
Places such as’ abound in the eastern
eng of Germany, which can be used for
ardly anything else. Beside the thread
material from the.stalk, the plants’ seeds
yield oil, and its roots nitrogen.

FOR TARIFF ON OUR GOWNS.

London Newspaper Advocates a
Duty, Conceding We Dictate Styles.

LONDON, April 15, (Correspondence
of The Associated Press.)—England hae
at last awakened to the fact that Amer-
ica hus become a’ great. power ih the

orld of fashion, and that many ideas
for women's apparel which formerly
came from France now emanate from
New York.

A London \ morning newspaper pub-
lishes a long editorial appealing to the
Government. to protect home industties
by clapping a heavy duty on styles im-
ported from New York. It says, in part:

“* Mepecially should we come down hot
and strong on American fashions. Our
French allies are concentrating their
energies on the war so closely that Paris
fashions have aimost ceased to exist,
and America is making frantic efforts
to establish herself as the maker of the

“'¥his is natural, but she may well be
made to pay for her opportunity. She
has always made France and England
pay tor dresses imported into the States,
and this is a very legitimate ocasion for
retaliation.

“It is hardly decent in war time for
women to wear fashionable dresses at
all, yet if the fashions came from Paris
we should find it difficult to place an
embargo on them.”

ney. The steamer was allowed to pro-
ceed after a short halt.

‘DR. BUTLER PLEADS

Tells of Disintegrating Elements
That Weaken Unity at Home
and Force Abroad.

MUST SET HOUSE IN ORDER

Editors at Meeting of Associated
Press Urged to Work for Free,
Powerful, Just America. *

Dr. * Nicholas Murray Butler, Presi-
dent of Columbia University, was the
principal speaker at. the annual lunch-
eon of The Associated Press yesterday
in the Waldorf. His-address in full fol-

Mr. President and Gentlemen of the
Associated Press:

For the honor of the invitation to be
your. guest . am deeply sensible, and
for that honor I wish first to express
my, grateful appreciation.. It is no
small compliment to be permitted to
speak at a time like this to a great
company of me drawn from all
parts of our nation, representing
every shade of opinion, who are sin-
gle-minded in their devotion to truth,
and to its interpretation as they seek
and understand it, and to our common
America. Mea

In this presence of men of affaits,

so closely in touch with the move-
ment of opinion all over the world,
accustomed to guide, to express, to
formulate it, there is nothing that I
can possibly say that you do not ai-
ready know. But I reflect that it is
out of the a geo of individuals,
and out of. their reaction to the chang-
ing course of events that first public
opinion, then history, is made.
- If any significance be attached to
what I shall briefly say in your pres-
ence, it can only be because it repre-
sents the attempt of one American
who feels keenly the responsibility of
his country and of the enwire citizen-
ship at this moment when the world
stands at a crossroads in its path of
progress.

If we stand at the crossroads ir-
resolute, paralyzed of will, history
will have one story to tell. If we turn
to the right and take the path that
leads upward to new achievement and
to lasting honor, it will have a very
different story to tell. If we should
turn to the left and follow the wind-
ing and rocky road that leads down
to a darkening gloom—we know not
where—histdry will have yet another
record to make of the American
people and of their capacity to repre-
sent civilization.

Leaders of Civilization.

It is just abot twenty years ago
since George Meredith, writing to The
London Daily News, said that since
the fortunate outcome of the greatest
of civil wars we have come to look
upon the American peopre as the lead-
ers -in civilization. That is a proud
and ennobling judgment, and we may
well search @ur minds and our hearts
to ascertain whether it be true, and
whether we are bey 3 mt for the
high honor that so distinguished an
observer of his kind proffered to us
as his personal judgment.

The question which I ask in your
presence this afternoon is this: ave
we an American nation? If ,so, is that
nation conscious of a unity purpose
and of ideals? If so, what is to be
the policy of that nation in the imme-
diate future? .

It must not be forgotten that na-
tions are comparatively new in human
history. There were no nations in the
ancient world. Men were grouped in
empires, in races, as followers of a
religion, as clansmen owing allegiance
to a chief, but not as nations as we
use the word. There were no nations
until the dream of a universal political
empire had passed away; until the
stately magnificence of Rome had
broken into a hundred fragments. It
was then and only then that a new
organizing force made itself felt in
the thoughts and deeds of men.

This new consciousness of unitv was
in part the outgrowth of unity of race
origin, in part the outgrowth of unity
of language, in part the outgrowth of
unity of institutional life, in part the
outgrowth of unity of military and
religious tradition. It seized hold of
the m‘nds of men in most practical
fashion. The result is that from the
time of the death of Charlemagne to
the time of the present German Em-

eror the history of the world is the
ters of nation building and the by-
products of nation building. A nation
is scientifically defined as a popula-
tion of an ethnic unity inhabiting a
geographic unity .under a common
form of government. The exceptions
are quite numerous enough to prove
this rule.

As the centuries have followed one
another it is not difficult to see how
the several nations have endeavored
to possess themselves of territory that
is a geographic unit. They have
sought natural boundaries, whether of
high mountains, cr of broad rivers, or
of the sea. itself. One War after an-
other is to be explained in terms of a
nation’s definite purpose to possess
itself of a geographic unity as its
home. ‘There has been by no means
equal care taken by the nations to es-
tablish and to protect an ethnic unity.
A strong~people has usually felt con-
fident that it could hold an alien ele-
ment in subjection and yet preserve
national integrity and unity of spirit.
So one after another of the greater
nations of the world has, in seeking
for geographic unity, insisted on in-
corporating in its own -body_ politic
alien and often discordant elements
and holding them in stern. subjection.
The examples are too familiar to be
recited here.

Nemesis of Nation Building.

This process of nation building has
gone on until the nation has come to
be conceived as an end in itself, as
superior to the law, to the conyentions
of morality, and to the precepts of re-
ligion. A form of patriotism his been
developed all over the world~ which
finds in the nation itself the highest

human end. The logical result, and
indeed the almost necessarv result, of
this type of thinking is the war which
. is now cremate over the world’s civ-
ilization and destroying it with the
sure pitilessness of an Alpine glacier.
This war is the nemesis of nation
building conceived as an end in itself.
Unless a nation, like an _ individual,
have sonie purpose, some ideal, some
motive which lies outside of and‘ be-
yond self-interest and self-aggrandize-
ment, war must. continue’ on the face
of this earth until the day when the
last and strongest man, superb in his
mighty loneliness, shall look out from
a rock in the Caribbean upon a world
that has been depopulated in its pur-

suit of a false ideal, and be left him- |

already stirring in the minds of west-

enteenth centuries. These aspirations
gained in force as the art of printing
aultiplied books and as the Samp =

Great Britain, Holland, France, were

America Not Yet a Nation.

On this Atlantic :shore distances
were great and communication *diffi-
cult.’ In addition there were social,
economic and religious differences that

kept the .struggling colonists apart.
The result was ‘that there grew up
heré: not a nation, but the ~material
out-of which-a nation could be made.

’ There is a-sense, a deep and striking

sense, in which the same ‘remains ab-
solutely true today: There is not yet
a nation, but the rich and fine ma-
terials Sut of which a true nation can
be made by the architects with vision
to plan and by the builder with skill
adequate to execute.

hen a common oppression forced
the separate colonists together they
still sadly lacked that devotion toa
unity higher than any of its component
parts, which would have saved so
much loss and ~ much suffering dur-
ing the days of revolution and of the
first steps toward a National Govern-
ment. An enormous step forward was
taken when the National Government
was built. In the adoption of the Con-
stitution of the United States the cor-
nerstone was laid for one of the most
splendid .structures in all the ‘history
of all nations. Then followed sharp
political divergence. There ‘were
those who wold iay stress upon the
new national unity; there were. still
more whe thought it important to em-
phasize the separate elements out of
which that unity had been composed.
The judicial logic of Marshall and the
convincing eloquence of Webster were
the chief unifying and nation-building
forces in the generation that followed.
Meanwhile sharp differences of eco-
nomic interests were manifesting
themselves, and the fatal question of
slavery pressed forwdrd both as an
economic and as a politf€al issue. The
new nation, which had already made
such progress upon the foundations
laid by the fathérs, feil apart, and
only after one of the most terrible
and destructive of civil wars were the
ruins of the disaster cleared away and
the ground prepared for the next step
in construction. Here mistakes were
made so numerous and so severe that
unifying and nation-building
process was checked and held back
for years. :

Then two sets of separating and dis-
integrating forces began to make
themselves strongly felt First, the
economic differences which must of
necessity manifest themselves over so
large and so diverse a territory now
reveal themselves in new force, in
part as a result of the industrial revo-
lution and in part as a result of pure-
ly American condition, as involving a
class conflict between capital and la-

r. Soon there were signs that citi-
zenship, with its compelling allegiance
to the common weal, wak to be subor-
dinated in discouraging ‘fashion, not
once but often, to the immediate in- .
— and policies of an economic
class.

Echo of Old World Feuds. /

Second, the immigration from all the
countries which had been for a long
time substantially homogeneous be-
came increasingly and rapidly hetero-
geneous. New nationalities, new, lan-
guages, new racial affinities were
drawn upon for the recruitment of the
population of the United States. The
hopes and the ambitions which 100

and 200 years before had been the pe-
culiar property of the people of West-
ern Europe had now spread far away
to the East and to the South. With
this heterogeneous immigration there
came, in no inconsiderable measure,
the echo of the Old World anizmosities
and feuds and hates. These did not
manifest themselves in any direct
sense as anti-American, but they did
manifest themselves with sufficient
strength to deprive America of a unity
of attitude, of feeling, and of policy
in dealing with international relations
which every day grew in importance
and in significance.

Se it is that at this moment, with a
world war raging about us and a
Presidential campaign openin in
front of us, with years full of fate
stretched out for us to'walk in, we
are not sure of our national unity of
thought and tectias and purpose be-
cause of the preSence of disintegrat-
ing elements and forces which weaken
our sense of unity at home and which
deprive us of the influence abroad
which attaches to unity at home. The
grave problem before the American
people today is that of completing the
process of nation pbuilding. It is the
bt of setting our house in order.
tis the problem of integrating Amer-
ca. It is the problem of subordinat-
ing every personal ambition, every
class interest and policy, every race
attachment, to the one dominant idea
of an America free, just, powerful,
forward facing, that shall stand out
in the history of nationg as the name
of: a people who conceive the mission
and their true greatness to lie in ser-
vice to mankind. We are the inher-
itors of a great tradition, What poets
and philosophers have eamed, that
we are trying day by day to do, our
stumblings, our blunders, our short-
comings are many; but if we keep our

our heads clear he

who a thousand years from now writes
the history of liberty and justice and
a eT among men will be able to
tell to those far-off generations the
story of the rise and influence of the
American: nation.

We find here everything. which -is
needed for a great nation. The. _

before the American people is

thing more nor less than a speed
continuation, and, if it be pra
the completion. of the proc
nation building. It is a problem of
the integration of America, about
those great fundamental principles
and purposes which the* very name
itself brings to our. mind and which
gg flag stirs to expression on every

Feel America in Our Hearts.

We know ‘in our hearts what
America means. The problem is to
teach it to our fellows; to share with
them an understanding and apprecia-
tion of it; to unite with them in an

expression of it that shall. give us an
America free, just, powerful, for-
ward facing; that shall conceive itself
as a nation fit to 'serve;-a nation

politic-which is new in conception, in
human. history, as it is new in its
own thought: of ‘its Perna: Can
America integrate itself at this crisis;
can it show that nere is a. nation
which ‘out of various and vari
ethnic elements can be created into a
genuine unity by devotion to high
principle and by moral purpose in the
face of all mankind? Can we have an
America that shall go down the cor-
ridors of time with a proud place on
the ‘pages of history?

We must remember that the greatest
empires have fallen as well.as risen.
We must remember that the most

‘ powerful dynastiés have passed away
as well as come into existence. There
is no reason suppose..that our
America is going to escape the ever-*
lasting law of change. e' know its
history and its origin. We have seen
its rise. We know its present state.
Who can predict how eer, hundreds
or thou ds of years it will.take be-
fore. the \forests will be felled and
the streams will dried, and this
great fertile continent of ours, like
the plains of ancient .tran, where
civilization began, become a ‘desert,
fit ‘only for ‘the surveying: parties of
the archaeologist?) When that time
comes, what do we want to have
written on the. pages of history of
, those who lived for “hundreds or per-
\haps-thousands of years on this con-
tinent? What do we want to have said
about the way in which America met
the greatest crisis of the world’s his-
tory in modern times,:in 1916? Do we
want a nation weak, broken to pieces,
irresolute, filled with conflicting and
discordant voices, or do We wish for
a nation unified, strong, sympathetic,
‘and ready to respond to the cause of
a common purpose. to serve all hu-
manity, even though the rest of hu-
manity be at war with itself?

Opportunity Knocking.

The year’1916 is but one member of
an infinite series. Countless aeons
have gone before it and countless
aeons will come after it. The. phy-

sical forces of nature will go their way
through indefinite time, performing
their alloted functions, obeying their
peculiar laws and undergoing those
manifold changes and transmutations
which make up the heavens and the
earth. Not se with the reputation
and the influence of a nation. Oppor-
tunity will not knock forever at any
door; it is knocking now at the door
of the American people. ;

If they are able to rise to a
ciation of their own part—of fits own
controlling principles and. pglitics, to
put aside every self-seeking, every
distracting, every brutal appeal—no
one can tell what lights will illumine
the page on which the history of our
nation may yet be written.

It is nearly sixty years since Abra-
ham Lincoln in his debates with Sen-
ator Douglas made mention of the
Scriptural sayi that ‘‘a house di-
vided against itself cannot stand,’’ and
he added, ‘‘ I do not expect the house
will fall, but I do expect the house
will cease to be divided."’

So Mr. President, I say today to this
influential company of Americans, we
do expect, every one of us, that our
house will cease to be divided. We
do expect that our America will come
to full consciousness of its purpose;
that the serene courage of Washing-
ton, the constructive genius of Hamil-
ton, the keen human insight and sym-
pathy of Jefferson, the patient pathos
of Lincoln, shall not have been in
vain in teaching us what our coun-
try 1s.

Shall we catch sight of that some-
thing higher than selfishness, higher
than material gain,-figher than the
triumph of brute force, which alone
can lead a nation up to those high
places that become sacred in history,
and from which influence descends in
a mighty torrent, to refresh, to vivify
and inspire all mankind?

It is as true today as it was in
ancient times, where there is no
vision the people perish. We can
make an America with a vision. We
cannot make it without. [Applause.]

FACES PRISON FOR A.KISS.

When Girl Screams Police Find
Counterfeiting Outfit.

Special to The New York Times,

PASSAIC,-N. J., April 25.—John Kupic,
28 years old, of 115 Tenth Street, at-
tempted to break into the apartments
of Miss Rose Somday at the same ad-
dress early this morning.

“Oh, Rose,’’ he is alleged to have
said, ‘‘ why can't you love me. I have
loads of money and we could be happy
together.’’

@ woman screamed for help, and
Policeman John Callahan arrested him.
Callahan found a trunk filled with fifty
counterfeit silver dollars and tools for

anufacturing counterfeit. coins in

ic’s room.

‘How. about . this?” the officer
asked, as he opened the trunk. ' “ Is-this
the source of your wealth? ’’

**A friend who collects such stuff gave
it all to me,’’ he answered.

In the City Court before Judge Thomas
P. Costello he pleaded guilty to the
charge of annoying Miss Somday, and
told the court that he only wanted to
kiss her,

He denied that he had made the cétun-
terfeit dollars, but he was turned over
to the Federal authorities. The police
think he is a member of a band of coun-
terfeiters.

MRdDEN CITY, N. Y., April 25.—Ger-
man methods of warfare received strik-

‘*How to stop the war we do not at

Our task is father to understand the

When the typhoid fever is raging in a

Not the cure, but the prevention of war,

I myself believe in adequate defense of
the fiation, éven though I may not be

tection again&t burglary, . cannot for a

80 long as I follow a Christ whose whole

Central Trust Co. to Auction Ivory

Set for 30 Years’ Storage.

Down fn the darkness, of a yault be-
néath Wall Street lie jumbled together
the kings and quéens and pawns and

ivory pieces lies the dust that has gath-

untouched by players’ fingers while the
courts of law“have tried to decide to
whom they belonged. With them in the
vault is the ivory-inlaid chessboard, also
a set of carved boxwood draughts.

But though the Central Trust Company
is an indulgent landlord to these aristo-
écrats of the ¢hessboard, it ipists on
payment of a thirty-year board ‘bill of
$560, and so on May 3 auctioneers will
stand on a table at 14 Vesey Street and
ask some one to pay the board bill of
the kings\and queens and knights and
pawns, However, before the purchaser
can take home the set he must pay
$111.50 on a ‘claim by Tiffany & Co.

Accérding*to Jotine, Larkin & Rath-
bone, lawyers, who yesterday advertised
the sale, Tiffany's in 1887 held the set
on a claim against John T. Howard,
Lyman B. Bunnell, and Moses Wiseman,

who, the lawyers said, were all dead
now, and when the three wished to
claim the set Tiffany’s found ;
claims against it, and refused to hand
it over. Mr. Howard bégan suit, which
resulted in the ¢ourt’s ordering Tiffany’s
to store the chessmen in a vault in the
then new building of the Central Trust
Company in Wall Street.

It was said yesterday at the offices of
the trust company that the chessmen
had remained isturbed in the same
vault since 1887. There has beén much
oe over who owned them, but in

ébruary of this year the Supreme
Court authorized the trust comeasy to
sell the royal echessmen for the thirty-
year board bill.

| XANZAC DAY” IN LONDON.

| King, Queen, and General Birdwood
at Services in Abbey.

| LONDON, April 25.—The anniversary
of the landing of the AuStralians and
New Zealand Army Corps on Gallipoli
Péninsula for the unsuccessful attempt
to capture the Dardanelles. was cele-
brated in London today by a parade
of Australasian soldiers and a memorial
service in Westminster Abbey. which
was conducted by the Dean of West-
minster. °

‘Dispatches from New Zealand and
Australia indicate that “Anzac Day,”
as the occasion is known, was celebrated
generally there by memorial and patri-
otic services.

The service at Westminster Abbey
was attended by the King and Queen
and by General Birdwood, who com-
manded the Australians and New
Zealanders throughout. tne campaign,
being described in an official dispaten|
as ‘‘the soul of the Anzac.” Official
representatives of Australia and New
Zealand also were in the audience, which
filled the great cathedral.
‘The parade to the Abbey gave Lon-
doners their first opporturfity since the
beginning of the war to cheer troops
safely returned from the front.

HOLLAND EATS WAR BREAD.

Submarines Cause Scarcity
American Wheat.

LONDON, April 25.—War bread ap-
peared on breakfast tables in Holland
for the first time this morning.

An Exchange Telegraph dispatch from
Amsterdam says that Dutch bakers
have been ordered to sell war bread on
account of the difficulty of procuring
American wheat. The scarcity is due to
submarine warfare and the. recent loss
of Dutch ships.

Funston to Accompany Him to Con-
ference with Obregon.

SAN ANTONIO, Texas, April 25.—
Generals Scott and Funston planned to-
day to leave tomorrow night for El Paso
to discuss with General Alvaro Obregon,
Secreta of War in the de facto ve
ernment Cabinet, the situation created
¥ the presence of American troops in

exico.

way north, will go to Juarez, opposite
El Paso, or to some other int on the
border has not been definitely stated,
and late today the War Department was
requested to ascertain and advise Gen-
eral Scott when the conference would
take place.

General Obrégon could get to Laredo
gr Bagle yf more quickly than to El

aso, but dispatches from Mexico City
and from Washington indicated that he
was going to, El Paso. To get there he
will have to pass through the United
States after entering either at Laredo
or Eagle Pass, or go through a district
between Torreon and Chihuahua that is

followers are not in actual control of
any great part of that district, they are
so numerous that the ge of Car-
ranza’s Minister of ar might be
dangerous unless he carried with him a
strong escort.

General Scott was advised by the War

structions concerning the character of
the discussion he is to have with
Obregon will be forwardéd to him to-
morrew.

that eight new machines “‘ of the latest
type ’’ were to be sent. “The four unh-
packed today, however, are tractors of

the same horse power as the ones that
have been wrecked. The engines are
rated at 90 horse power, and are said
to develop less. The new machines have
greater wing surface than the old, but
this is said to be a drawback in this
counsy of tregcherous air currents, as
it diminishes speed.

with Strike of Government Help.

A of the Fourteenth United States In-
fantry stationed at Fort Liscum, near
here, hat been ordered to Anchorage
for patrol duty in connection with the
strike of laborers employed in the con-

struction of the Government railroad.
The soldiers will sail. for Agchorage
Wednesday on the steamship Alaska.

M. Brown and Assistant District At-
torney Munley have gone to Anchorage
in response to a telegram from Lieu-
tenant Frederick Mears of the Alaska,
Engineering Commission, requesting
their presente in connection with the
strike. situation. .

Lane requésted the War Department to

ROBBER KILLS POLICEMAN.

Two Others Badly Injured in Pistol
Duel Fought in Cincinnati.

CINCINNATI, Ohio, April 25.—In a
desperate pistol battle in the heart. of
Cincinnati’s business district at noon
today, Patrolman Samuel Robbins was
shot and killed, a pawnbroker named
Louis Katz was probably fatally shot,
while William Groendike, 20, of Car-
thage, Ohio, accused by the police of
doing the shooting, was in turn shot
and probably fatally wounded by De-
tective Albert Wegener.

The police assert that Katz was shot
when Groendike ettempted to hold up
the pawnbroker in his shop, that Groen-
dike opened fire when Robbins hurried
to aid Katz, after the latter called for
pelp. and that Wegener, seeing his fel-
1 Fain fall, immediately shot Groen-

Henry T. Draper of 245 East 128d
Street, was born a British subject and
became a citizen of the United States
in 1890. He was asked by Henry M.
Unger, of Fay’s counsel, whether his

as he was now—‘thank God’’—an
American citizen. He said he had never
dealt in ‘* war brides,’’ and that he had
read about the Fay case in a Harlem

1 in. the box until late in the afternoon,

trict Attorney's office. He is counsel for
Darche.

with Mild Condenfation.
Judge Julius M. Mayer filed yesterday.

randum in a proceeding entitled -‘‘ In the
Matter of an Attorney.’’ His action fol-
lowed the recéipt by him of a report
from Samuel Owen Edmonds; Chairman
of the Committee of Discipline of the
New York County Lawyers’ Association,
on charges lodged against the unnamed
attorney. ‘
’ gone dl to this report the defendant,
man. experience and of . mature
tely violated a stiputa-

and opposing counsel with the view of
ting before the jury the facts which

‘The committee that investigated: re-

“It is the opinion of your sub-com-
mittee that a st Loge breach of. obliga-
tion, undertaken by an. attorney to the
court, such.as is here disclosed, is a
serious dereliction and should not pass
uncondemned, . The circumstances 6f

that the measure of the penalty that
shouldbe inflicted and the method. of

Gold Watch for Vasari’s Captain.

The Lamport & Holt steamship Vasari,
which. arrived on Saturday from Buenos
Aires, left yesterday for Liverpool with
40,157 quarters of Argentine beef in her
refrigerators. On the voyage up from
South America the passengers collected
a purse of $250 to present Captain Oscar
Penrice with a gola watch and chain
on his fiftieth birthday, which was yes-
terday. As they could not purchase a

ld watch and chain on the Vasari the

"sun carved one out of a Bahia ivory
nut, which was handed to Captain Pen-
rice-at dinner-on Friday night, and the
real watch was presented to him yester-
day by a committee of the passengers
just before the Vasari left her pier\near
Montague Street, Brooklyn.

hand just what a certain trucking cost

FOULED W. U. CABLES.
Stockholm. Obeyed Strange Tig-
boat’s Order to Anchor.
Obeying an unauthorized order from
an unidentified tugboat Captain to
anchor his ship instead of proceeding to
the pier in Jersey City, Captain. A. E.
Hakanson of the Swedish-American
liner Stockholm, which arrived -yester-
day. ftom Gothenburg, fouled three
Western Union cables off Pier B, Jer-

two hours in the North River.. The
cable repair steamer Western Union
was sent for and her crew managed to
get the cables clear from-the flukes of
the liner’s anchor.

The Stockholm left Gothenburg on
April 11 and was taken into Kirkwall
by a British cruiser and detained three
days. Her 485 bags of mail were taken
ashore for examination and. brought
back and then taken ashere a second
time and returned.

' On Palm Sunday, April 16, in the
midst of a westerly gale, Mrs. Bertha
Bjorkman gave birth to a baby girl in
the third-class, who was christened
Stockholmina after the ship. It was
the first birth on’ the Stockholm, and
the Captain had mother and child re-
moved to a cabin de luxe in the first-
class, and presented her with 300
kronen on behalf of the rr: The
passengers added another ronen,
which made up a purse of $216 for Mrs.
Bjorkman to receive when she is able
to leave the ship and start to join her
husband at 1,639 Ballou Street, Chicago.

The agents of the line have not been
able to identify the Captain of the tug-
boat--which gave instructions, to the

Stockhoim off Liberty Island not to go
to her plier.

To Debate Preparedness Problems.
Mrs. Bertha H. Mailly, Secretary of
the Rand School of Social Science, last
night denied that the National Security
; League had turned down the challenge
to debate a Socialist on the question of
preparedness at the Labor Pageant to be
given at the Central Opera House for
four days beginning next Friday night.
A similar denial was made by Robert
Grimshaw, Chairman of the Speakers’
| Bureau of the National Security League,
inc. Mrs. Mailly said that the commit-
tee had agreed to have a preparedness
speaker meet a Socialist in debate on
: question of the ‘* Relation of Prepared-
‘ness to the Cause of Labor.”’ In a letter
| to Mrs. Mailly yesterday Mr. Grimshaw
accepted the challenge and stated that
the league would gladly furnish speakers
in any language desired.

PITTSBURGH, April 25. ety e's that
the National Guard might be called out
to preserve order, owing to the strike of

ity chained fron gates at two entrances
rushed past private guards, and entered
the plant in an effort to persuade work-

No arrests were made.

Pickets at the electric plant this morn-
ing attempted to prevent several thou-
sand workmen from entering. A clash
with Deputy Sheriffs and railroad de-
tectives followed, but no one was seri-
ously hurt.

INDIANS BEAT WHITE SOX.

Five Chicago Pitchers Sacrificed on
Dunn Day in Cleveland.

CLEVELAND, April 25. — Cleveland
defeated Chicago here today in the
opening game of the series, 9 to 2. Chi-
cago used five pitchers and the two
left handers, Russell and Williams, were
the only ones to show any effective-
ness. Coumbe, who pitched for Cleve-
land, held Chicago to six hits, three of
which were made by Fournier. He gave
‘passes to the firat two batters in the
fourth, and the recipients of those
favors were the only Chicago men to
gcore.- 2
“The Woodland Bards of Chicago were
present in honor of their fellow-mem-
ber, James C. Dunn, President of the
Cleveland Club, the day being desig-
nated as ‘‘ Dunn Day.’’ The Bards were
guests of the Cleveland Chamber or
Commerce at luncheon, which was fol-
lowed by an automobile parade to the
baseball park. Two bands of music
were on hand and Dunn was presented
with a large wardrobe trunk by the
Cieveland Fire Department. Among the
well-known men present were Secretary
of War Baker, B. B. Johnson, President
of the American League; Charles Comis-
key, owner of the Chicago White Sox,
and Charles Weeghman, owner of the
Chicago Cubs. The score:

HONOR TWO TRAPSHOOTERS

Local Marksmen Bid Adieu to Laca-
telli and Yule.

Lieutenant Ercole H. Locatelli, an: im-
porter of this city, who has two broth-
ers serving in the Italian Army, is to
sail on May-17 to join his regiment.
During his twelve years’ sojourn in New
York he has made a record at the traps.
and the White Plains Gun Club arranged
in his honor a farewell testimonial
shoot, which was held yesterday at the
Gedney Farms traps. Tom Davis, on
behalf of the club, gave Lieutenant Lo-
catelli a souvenir in the shape of a wrist
watch, which he will wear at the front.

The New. York Athletic Club tra
shooters also gave Locatelli and W.
Yule, another crack shot who won the
championship at Boston last week, a
farewell dinner at the club last night.
Mr. Yule is leaving New York for Ohio.
Each guest of honor received a dia-
mond-studded mercury foot, presented
by Danny McMahon. Mr. Yule’s souve-
nir from the White Plains Gun Club was
a shotgun case.

Forty-four men faced the traps in
yesterday’s shoot, and they made some
remarkable scores. Thirty of them re-
turned scores of 90 or better, and ten
others did better than 80.

Ralph L. Spotts, in winning the high
scratch prize, made a_run of 75 clean
breaks. In the next 25 he missed only
one target. The high handicap prize
was won*by D. F. McMahon with a
total of 100 on his handicap of 4. He
made a straight run of 54. There were
six handicap prizes, and they were won
in the following order: Captain W. H.
Dreyer, 8S. P. illiams, J. Schirmer, B.
E. Eldert, Dr. G. H. Martin, and M.
MecVoy, Jr.

NO FREE GOLF TRAIN.

Amateurs Who Play in Western
Tourney, Must Pay Their Fare.

SAN FRANCISCO, April 25.—No spe-
cial train wall carry Eastern golfers west
‘free of ¢xpense to compete in the West-
érn amateur championships tournament,
to be held at Del Monte, Cal., in July, it
became known here today. The Cali-
fornia Golf Association has sent a com-
munication to the Western Golf Associa-
tion stating that it agreed to abide by
the decision of the latter organization
not to accept the free train which was
offered by the Californians. The train
was declined because, it was held, its
acceptance would constitute a violation
of the amateur rule.

NO MORE CUSHION FIGHTS.

Hurlers of Mats at Chicago Cubs’
Park Will Be Arrested.

CHICAGO, April 25.—Patrons of the
Chicago National League Park who en-
gage in cushion fights will be arrested,
it was announced today ,by Charles
Weeghman, President of the club, after
a conference with police officials.

Several.women have been injitred as
a result of being struck by cushions
hurled over the crowd by enthusiastic
spectators. Damages have been sought
by the victims. Sufficient police to ar-
rest all cushion hurlers henceforth will
be stationed at the park, Mr. Weegh-
man said.

COLLRGE met |

Association Formed to Provide
Athletic Facilities for Many
_ Busy Women.

More than 200 college women met last
night in the assembly hall of the Met-
ropelitdn Building to launch the first
Intercollegiate Alumnae Athletic Asso-
ciation, the object of which is the fur-
nishing of exercise and recreation to
college women iff and near New York
under inexpensive and congenial con-
ditions. The new association is really
an outgrowth of the activities carried
on among college. women by the Alum-
nae Committee on Athletics of Barnard
College. It started in 19183 with a mem-

rship of twenty-five women, and now
the figures show 975. enrolled members.

Those who were actiye in college ath-
letics during their undergraduate days
felt, after many of them had entered
upon business careers, that some plan
might be arranged whereby their leis-
ure hours could be devoted in part to
athletic exercise. In furtherance of this
the original organization was formed.
Outdoor and indoor sports were featured,
horseback riding, basket ball, swim-
ming, folk dancing, gymnasium work,
and the like being taken up. Teachers’

women one night weekly,
riding occupied another, and hockey,
tennis, baseball, yachting, &c., also
played a part in the ee ce
The organization became

horseback

popular

collegiate Alumnae Athletic Association.
Miss Lillian Schoedler, a Barnard grad-
uate of 1911, who was prominent in
athletics as an undergraduate, has been
one of the prime movers in bringing
cbcut the formation of the new asso-
ciation,

*Miss Schoedler was Chairman of. the
meeting last night.. Among the speakers
were Miss Constance Applebee, head of
the Physical Education Department of
Bryn Mawr, and Dr. Kristine Mann,
head of the Department Store Educa-
tional Association.

Following a dinper last night the fol-
lowing officers were elected : President—
Miss Elsa Alsberg. Barnard; First Vice
President—Miss- Elsie Detmold, Smith ;
Second Vice President—Miss Margarette
Dainels, Mount Holyoke; Secretary—
Miss Agnes Morrow, Bryn Mawr; Treas-
urer—Miss Lucille Cochran, ‘Vassar;
Auditor—Miss Susan Van Wert, Cornell ;
Executive Secretary—Miss Katharine
Ecob, Bryn Mawr; Chairman of the
Committee on Indoor Athletics—Miss
Marion Halsey, Smith; Chairman of the
Committee on Outdoor Athletics—Miss
Edith Cassett, Mount Holyoke; Chair-
man of the Committee on Horseback
Riding—Miss Margie Hoffman, Barnard;
Chairman of the Membership Committee
—Miss Elizabeth Meigs, Purdue.

The colleges represented in the new
association are Barnard, Smith, Mount,
Holyoke, Vassar, Wellesley, Brown,
Goucher, Bryn Mawr, Oberlin, Wiscon-
sin, Elmira, Adelphi, Cornell, "Randolph
Macon, Wells,. Iowa State. Bates, Maine,
Florida State, Ohio Wesleyan, Boston
University, Minnesota, Dickinson, Prince
of Wales, (Canada.) Swarthmore, Cali-
fornia, Bucknell, Radcliffe. Cincinnati,

SLOOP PAULINE SAILS WELL.

Nat Herreshoff Gives New 40-Footer
a Spin Off Bristol.

Special to The New York Times,
BRISTOL, R.. 1, April 25.—Swinging
full sail in a grayback southwester this
afternoon the sloop Pauline, the second
of the New York Y. C. forty-foot class
yachts Jaunched at’ Herreshoff's, re~
ceived a searching test today from Nat
Herreshoff,, the designer. Pauline left
her mooring with club topsatl and jib
topsail spread over lower gails, Herre-
shoff holding the wheel as the craft
Sathered headway and heeled gently

. Passing Poppas Quash with wind
abeam, Herreshoff jammed the Pauline
sharp on the’ wind when she began to
show gratifying speed. The sails were

a elose haul. The sloop behaved ~ better
in consequence, held a course very close
to the wind, and legged it across Narra-
gansett Bay in fine “ye to ‘sands Point
Light.

Herreshoff imancateeed the bias toa
reach without starting the main sheet.
A close search of the hull and. top~
hamper for weak s was made, but
none was discovered.

After a run up the bay to Providence
Point the designer threw out more kinks
by jibing ‘with sheets aft. In each
manoeuvre the Pauline behaved finely
and stood firmly to the breeze. It is
doubtful if three professionals will be
sufficient to handle these craft, which
go in ateye like. machines.

SOCCER PROTEST REJECTED.

Continentals Not Upheld in Matter
of Eligibility of Swords.

T. W. Cahill, Secretary of the United
States Football Association, announced
yesterday that the Natiorlal’ Challenge
Cup Committee had not sustained the
protest of the Continental Football Club
of New York against the Fall River
Rovers, the winners of the recent @natch
in the semi-final round of the annual
cup-tie competition at Pawtucket.

The Continentals protested on the
ground that T. Swords was ineligible to
play. From evidence submitted it ap-
peared that Swords had been stfispended
from playing‘in league games, but, un-
der the rules of the Southern New Eng-
land Association, was still eligible to
play in cup-ties. While their claim was
rejected, the Continentals got back their
protest fee, while the Fall River Rovers
were fined $25 for infraction of Rule
7 of the U. S. F. A. by-laws in not
furnishing a complete list of their play-
ers ten days before the semi-final game.

The Fall River Rovers will now meet
the Bethlehem Footbail Club in the final
round for the cup at Pawtucket, R. I.,
on Coates Field, on May 6. The follow-
ing officials have been selected for the

ame: Referee, David M. Whyte of

rooney linesmen, aes Mitchell of

New Bedford and J. Booth of Bridgeport ;

delegates, George M. Collins of ton
and Andrew M. Brown of New York.

Atlantic Fleet.

ders for the immediate organization of
a new division of submarines for the
Atlantic fleet, to be made up of vessels
just completed or nearing completion.
It will be known as the Fifth Division
and will. comprise the M-1, which is the
largest submarine ever built for the
navy, and four of the ‘new boats of the
L class. The L boats in the division

Arnold Daly, a gifted player and a

bold one, has launched at the Cort
Theatre, in: West Forty-eighth Street, a
revival of ‘‘ Beau Brummell,’’ the youth-
ful work of Clyde Fitch of which the
central and all-obscuring réle made a
fortune for Richard Mansfield and is
more closely identified with the popular
memory of that great actor than any
other of the many parts he played. The
play, which has been.vigorously brushed
up in preparation for its reappearance
on the stage, wears surprigingly well,
and would provide a highly entertaining
evening in the theatre if Mr, Daly him-
self were to gi 2 a more digtinguished,
delicate, and 4maginative’ performance
as the ultimate dandy.

Mr. Daly is an actor of too keen in-
telligence and too considerable skill to
make an utter botch of any part, but his
playing as the Beau is disappointing to
his admirers, doubly disappointing, of

pared it must be, with the long-familiar
playing of Mansfield in this part, which,
ordered liké a coat, was cut to his meas-
ure, and which fitted him like a glove.
The playgoer is a creature whose memo-
ries grow distorted and half obliterated
as season succeeds season, and Mr. Daly
would be challenging a phantom if Mans-
field had merely played ‘‘ Beau Brum-
mell’’ twenty-six years ago and passed
on to something else: But he played it
up to the year of his death, and his de-
lightful performance in the part is
among the ‘‘ memories and portraits "’
of the last ten years.

Mr. Daly's Brummell would more pro-
foundly impress a bling playgoer. His
voice is a highly effective instrument,
and its William Gillette-like note of
world weariness, of elegant boredom, is
ever so helpful in the politely contempt-
uous speeehes of the fastidious Beau.
But his appeararce in his present make-
up is most unfortunate. He is quite hor-
ridly bewigged, and even in his most
gorgeous raiment gives rise to faint and
disturbing meniories of marked-down
Hamlets, of comic-paper tragedians
walking wearily on the ties.

All this makes his way harder in the
acts, where he is iess ef-
fective and, thus handicapped, he plays
the Beau without enough of that grace,
elegance, and supreme distinction which
would lend plausibility to the comedy
and add laurels to his brow. Arnold
Daly has so far departed from his prac-
tice as to do a piece of work in a quite
commonplace manner.

He jis not buoyed up by a brilliant and
well-directed company, although Stan-
ley Dark and William Raymond givé
good accounts of themselves. It was Mr.
Dark who staged the revival and, ac-
cording to the program, prepared the
text for performance in the year of
grace 1916,

The process of revision has been vijt-
orous. Gone are the old asides ar
soliloquies, and the alterations hav
not stopped there. The first act has
been split into two scenes, the last com-
pressed into one. Mariana is on her
way to him when he dfés; but the King
and his friends at Court never visit
him at Calais. They enter the last act
only us spectral memories of the grand-
eur that was Brummell, appearing only
in his vision when, in the midst of his
pathetic phantom supper, the wall of
his garret in Calais grows suddenly
transparent, and he. sees them all (as
you do) at table, and hears them toast-
ing him. These revisions are all for
the better, and as the dying Beau, Mr.
1. strikes fire.

eau Brummell ”’ shows its age, but
time has dealt gently with it, and its
slignty farchaic structure seems now,
75 uaint, scarcely distinguishable,
and rather pleasing part. of its own
backward glance to the leisurely days
of a hundred years ago. This whet
too, will blend pleasantly w that
pleasure of memory which, Tor many
playgoers, | will be part of the pleasure
of seeing ‘‘ Beau Brummell ”’ at the Cort
—to see the Beau walk in the Mall and
hear him say once more, ‘‘ Wales, will
you ring the bell’’ or “Sherry, who’s
your fat friend? ’’ Certainly the audience
which filled the Cort ‘last evening
seemed to be having a good time. There
was much applause, and, in his fashion,
Mr. Daly made @ little speech.

MME. FARRAR HAS QUINSY.

Confined to Her Home Here—Gatti-
Casazza May Not Go Abroad.

‘Geraldine Farrar, instead of being
with the Metropolitan Opera Company
in Atlanta, Ga., this week, as was in-
tended, is at her home in New York,
suffering from quinsy sore throat.
is confined to her room and under a
physician's care, Mme. Farrar's illness
first became known to the public last
week, when a performance of ‘‘ Madama
Butterfly,” scheduled for Wednesday
evening in Boston, had to be postponed
on her account. She came home then
and has been there ever since. Her
candition is not regarded as_ serious

ee: the viewpoint of her general

General Manager Gatti-Casazza is now
in his office at the Opera House every
day for the first time eke the Russian
Ballet took possession there. It is very

robable that the director, for ‘the first
irne since he has been connected with
the institution, will not go abroad dur-
ing the Summer to hear singers. He
found it very difficult last Summer to
make arrangements for meeting artists,
as even with headquarters in neutral
Switzerland there were difficulties
about artists and director reaching each
other. This Summer the situation is
more complicated than before, and it is
doubtful as to how much could be ac-
complished by Mr. Gatti-Casazza leav-
ing the United States. He has not yet
decided positively.

On Mondey he will make known the
personnel of the company for next sea-
son, with whatever has been. definitely
decided already as to new productions
and other plans for the next season.

3 PRIZE CANTATAS SUNG.

Paterson Music Festival Opens to
3,000—Anna Case a Soloist.

Special to The New York Times.

PATERSON, N. J., April 25.—Three
thousand lovers of good music crowded
the Fifth Regiment Armory here tonight
at the opening ‘‘ American”’ night of
the Paterson music festival.“ Miss Anna
Case, soprano of the Metropolitan Opera
Company, was heard in several num-
bers, among them “ Sacred Fire,’”’ by
Alexander Russell; ‘“‘ A Hindu Slumber
Song,”’ by Harriet Ware; MacDowell’s
‘* Slumber Song,” ‘‘ That’s the World in

June,’’. by Charles Gilbert Spross, and
*“ Bird of the Wilderness,” by Edward
Horsmaan.

The festival chorus of 1,000 voices ren-
dered three prize cantatas, written espe-
cially for the festival. hey were
* Onowa,” first prize, by Franz Born-
schien; ‘‘ America,’’ second prize, by
Carl Busch, and “‘ Miracle of Time,’’ by
W. Franke Harling. In the latter num-
ber 500 school children sang in the
chorus.

Merle Alcock rendered several con-
tralto solos, her best being the prologue,
‘* Iphigenia in Aulis."’
‘* Love’s Anguish,’’ by Mary
Brown; ‘‘ Unremembered,”’ by F. Morris
Class, and ‘‘ Flower Rain,” by John
Adams Loud. Anton de Vally, a Bel-
gian tenor, who lately artived in_ thi
country, pleased. C. Mortimer Wiske
conducted the several orchestra num-

bers.
The festival will continue’ with

EMBARGO ON NEW HAVEN.

Situation Less Serious Than
March, Officiale Assert.

The New York, New Haven & Hart-
ford, on which a freight embargo was
lifted recently, has again accumulated
on its tracks more cars than can be
profitably handled. As a result an em-
bargo was declared yesterday, effective
at midnight Thursday, on all bituminous
and anthracite coal, upon lumber and
cement consigned to Waterbury, Hart-
ford and Torrington, and, to a limited
extent, to all other places, and: on all
less than cargo freight, with the excep-
tion of foodstuffs for human consum
tion, printing paper, household goods,
and freight for the United States Gov-
ernment.

It was.officially declared, however,
that the situation is by no means as
acute as it was during March, and that
measures have been taken whereby the
situation may be,kept well in hand
through the loading of cars to the
maximum capacity. The number of cars
held py other roads for New Haven a
ritory has been reduced from 25,000 t
9,000 since the organization of the Con-
ference Committee.

Harkness. Estate Hearing June 9.

An application made in behalf of State |
Controller Travis to have Lamon V.
Harkness, who left an estate of an es-
timated valife of more than $100,000,000,
declared a resident of the. State of New
York at the time of his death came up
yesterday before Surrogate Cohalan, and
the hearing was adjourned until ‘June
9, upon the request of William W. Win-

ate, special attorney for the Controller.
The’ Controller will try to show that the
estate is taxable in this State under the
transfer tax law.

MANN THE OBSTRUCTIONIST.

The belief of Mr. Mann of Illinois
that we should have a regular army
of 250,000 men is of less importance
to the country than the fact that, by
obstructive tactics, he succeeded in de-
laying action on the Military bill a
whole week. The Senate passed the
bill on Tuesday of last week. Con-
ferees should have been appointed at
once and the work of the Conference
Committee might have been finished
in less time than was required to
overcome Mr. MANN’s opposition to a
special rule by which to expedite pro-
ceedings. Yesterday his resistance was
thrust aside.

We cannot fairly accuse Mr. Hay or
the Democrats of adopting obstruc-
tionist tactics because they would not
assent to a final vote on the bill with-
out a conference. The eminent par-
liamentarian’ who lately disgusted
even his own party by his injudicious
and entirely partisan criticism of
President Witson’s speech to Con-
gress on the German situation was the
obstructionist. He knew perfectly well
that his proposal would be rejected by
the majority. He is strong for pre-
paredness, but he wants it to bear an
exclusively Republican stamp.

THE BRITISH BLOCKADE AND
NEUTRAL RIGHTS.

We have pointedly refused to mix up
the two unrelated questions of Ger-
many’s slaughter of American citizens
and England’s hampering of American
trade when the Berlin Government
made a suggestion to that effect. It is
plain, therefore, that we cannot act
affirmatively upon the proposal made
.by the British Government in the note’
published this morning, that we join
with other neutral nations in an effort
“to prevent the violation of neutral
rights,” since such a joint commission
would nattrally have to concern itself
first of all with the gravest class of
offenses, those committed by German
submarines, and then with blockade
These are questions which
‘we must take up separately, in our own
time and in our own Way.

The spirit of candor and friendliness
in which the London note discusses
interferences with trade is manifested
in the declaration, now made to us for
the second time, that the Orders in
Council. do. not control the British
prizé courts. | Those tribunals are free
to declare illegal acts in contravention
of internationa]. law, and aggrieved

blockade binding upon neutrals.

The figures of our greatly swollen
exports to neutral countries from
which Germany is supposed to receive
goods that thus evade thé blockade
are too convincing to admit of much
dispute. Besides, in the packers’ cases
it was openly admitted in the prize
court that goods shipped to Sweden
and Denmark had Germany as their
real destination. Once more England
cites in justification of her acts our
own blockade procedure and the de-
cisions of our courts during the civil
war. Like cases call for like law. All
will be diligently scrutinized for un-
likeness. We have.as a present re-
lance for freedom from molestation
for our commerce the announctd pur-
pose of the Allies to minimize delays
and “make their restraints on’ trade
“as little burdensome to neutrals as
“ possible.” Beyond that is the appeal
to international iw in prize court ad-
judication of acts done under the
municipal law of Great Britain and

France.

THE KAISER’S CAPSTICK.

The Fifth New Jersey District is
represented in the Sixty-fourth Con-
\eress by JoHN H. CapsTicK, Repub-
lican. It should be-represented in the
Sixty-fifth Congress by an American.

Mr. CapPsTicK has just received from
the loyal subjects of the Empire in
Union County and way stations this
testimonial to his-sacrifice of mere
American rights to the German vote:

Honorable Sir: At the regular meet-
ing of. the German-American Alliance
of Elizabeth and vicinity, twenty-
four societies, consisting of 2,300 vot-
ing members, a resolution was passed
to offer you a vote of thanks and
sincere appreciation for your action in
voting for the McLemore resolution,
by which “we are convinced you are
intent upon retaining friendly relations
between the United States and Ger-
many.

“ Retaining friendly relations” is the
Elizabethan translation of _“ meekly
“consenting to the murder of Amer-
“ican citizens.” The German-Amer-
ican Alliance pledges itself to support
heartily the Kaiser’s faithful CapsTIcK
in his campaign. “ We are all of opin-
ion,” says an official of the New Jer-
sey German-American Alliance, “ that
“the Administration wants to,have war
“with Germany.”

In 1914 Mr. Capstick got 16,951
votes, the Democratic candidate 15,718,
the Progressive candidate 2,218. The
district \was, and ordinarily is, Repub-
lican. There used to be a number of
Americans in it. They must be proud
of CaPSsTICK.

BUCHANAN or Senator SHERMAN. “It

TOPICS OF THE TIMES.

Charity, seeking, as
charity must, an ex-
Sir Roger planation that will
Casement. serve as an excuse
for a crime as ab-
horrent to all the world as treason,
finds first and only the possibility that
Sir Roger CaskMENT was a victim of the
neurasthenia that so often diminishes or
destroys the moral responsibility of men
who stay too long and work too hard in
the tropics. That he was in some degree
a sufferer from that dread malady is,
indeed, more than a _ possibility--it is a
probability, as much of Sir Rogsr’s time
for twenty years had been passed in
parts of the world where men of his
breed and type can remain with im-
punity only when they carefully refrain
from exhausting activities of mind and
*body.

However, the desire for the sake of
humanity's self-respect to palliate this
man’s treachery is weakened by the
knowledge that, throughout his career
in the Consular service, though he was
living on British pay and had accepted
a title and. other honors from the
British Government, he had always been
a bitterly hostile critic of the’ Empire
that employed him, and his principal
and doubtless congenial achievement was
the conduct of an investigation the re-
sult of which brought deep and deserved
humiliation on all Englishmen.

The Germans, with characteristic in-
ability to understand the state of public
sentiment outside of their own country,
seem at first to have expected him to be
La useful tool for use against their most
hated enemies. His complete failure to
accomplish anything of value for them
soon made him almost as coldly viewed
in Berlin as at home, and his condition
for months past has been one of tragic,
almost pathetic, loneliness. What his
position was in the absurd and inevitably
disastrous expedition that ended in his
capture is not revealed, but it could
hardly have been one of more than con-
temptuous toleration. For him, with his
knowledge, to take part in such a futile
scheme hints at desperation. It was a
sort of suicide, for the plea of insanity,
the only plea his friends can make, is
unlikely to save him.

Fate of

A new definition of
what constitutes hon-
esty in advertising
has been provided by
the United States Su-
Preme Court in a truly interesting case
that came to it from Southern Florida.
There, it seems, a real estate company
had been sefling land to more or less
guileless investors, presumably North-
ern. It had charged them prices that
appear to have been reasonably, or at
least decently, near to what the land
was worth for the uses to which it
could be put. This, a Florida court held,
.made the transactions legitimate, but the
Wise Men in Washington gave a considy
eration that had been refused by their
humbler brothers to the fact that though
the buyers of the land got their money’s
worth, they did not get land valuable in
the ways that the company’s advertise-
ments had promised and justified them
in expecting.

Therefore the Supreme Court held the
tfansactions to be, not legitimate, but
fraudulent. ,

It is interesting, and even a little
amusing, to notice that in the opinion
as rendered there appears, incidentally,
a kindly concession to human nature as
it is, and a truly judicious recognition
of a weakness in it too nearly universal
to be condemned. The decision, to be
more explicit, refrains—and carefully
says that it refrains—from declaring
fraudulent the high-pitched praise by
the seller of wares with which all men,
since men began to barter together, have
been accustomed to meet an opposite
tendency of buyers toward depreciation
of the other fellow’s goods,

Of course exaggeration of merit, from
the standpoint of the strict and rigid
moralist, is not right, but, whether nec-
essary or not, the world’s experience
has shown it to be inevitable, and im-
memorial custom gives it a sanction
which the law does well not to deny. If
hard pressed, the Supreme Court would
probably say that the exaggerating done
by the seller, to escape the taint of
fraud, must have a certain sincerity and
be done.with a certdift moderation. As
it was, *however, the court didn’t go even
that far; it was content to say. that ex-
aggeration was one thing and lying an-
other, though the two are near neigh-
bors and close acquaintances, and to let
the sleeping dog of a question lie undis-
turbed.

MEYER LONDON A MINORITY

Technical Parliamentary Ruling De-
nounced ‘by “Mann. as Unfair—
Conferees,for Preparedness.

Special to The New York Times.

WASHINGTON, April 25.—Ending the
fight of the-Republican minority to in-
struct the conferees of the lower cham-~
ber to accept the Senate amendment
for an army of 250,000 men, the House
today sent to conference the Army Re-
organization bill and failed to record
itsef on the “big army ’”’ issue. :

A peculiar parliamentary situation,
wherein Representative Meyer London
of New York, the lone Socialist mem-
ber, was recognized to. make a motion
to recommit the bill, ‘was the undoing
of the Republican plans for a record
vote on the big army amendment, Rec-
ognition of Representative London. by
Speaker Champ Clark at a time when
the Republicans were seeking to recom-
mit the bill and instruct the Military
Committee to accept the Senate amend-
ment so displeased Representative Mann,
the Republican floor leader, that for the
first time he seriously questioned a rul-
ing by Speaker Clark.

‘““That is an unfair ruling,’’ said Mr.
Mann, when the Speaker held that Mr.
London was the only House member
entitled to make the recommittal mo-
tion. The rules require that a mem-
ber moving fo recommit must announce
his unqualified opposition to the bill.

Representative Julius Kahn, ranking
Republican of thé Military Committee,
had demanded prior recognition to move
to send the Army bill to the committee
and instruct it to disagree to all Sen-
ate amendments except that relating to
the army of 250,000 men. Representa-
tives Harrison, Foster, and CNsp, Dem-
ocrats, raised the point of order that
Mr. Kahn was not entitled to make a
motion to recommit. The Californian,
they said, could not be opposed to the
entire bill, and therefore did not come
within the rule. The speaker decided
that Mr. Kahn did not bring himseif
within the rule and that Mr. London,
opposing, as he did, all forms of army
legislation, should be recognized.

‘‘The minority is entitled to move to
recornmit,”’ said Speaker Clark, ‘‘ and
Mr. London is a minority party all by
himself.’”’ ‘

Mr. London’s motion to recommit
made no reference to the 6ize of the
army. He wes the only member to vote
for his motion, the vote being 248 to 1.

Conferees for Big ,Army.

The Speaker named as_ conferees
Chairman Hay and Representative Dent,
Democrats, and Répresentative Kahn,
Republican, of the Military Affairs
Committee. Subsequently the Senate
named as conferees Senators Chamber-
lain, Beckham, and Broussard, Demo-
crats, and Warren, ex-Chairman of the
committee, and du Pont, Republicans.
On the whote, the Conference Commit-
tee is regarded as favorable to a big

rmy.

*'The House adopted the rule sending
the army bill to conference 208 tod 146.
This was not generally regarded as a
test vote ag between the ‘“ big army
and “small army” adherents. Both
sides expected later to have a show-
down vote on the Senate amendment,
and this failed to materialize.

Debate preceding the disposition of
the army bill developed tharp differ-
ences over preparedness. The greatest
ovtburst of applause came when the
Republican leader, Mr. Mann. said:

“T want the United States to keep
out of the war. I am opposed even to
breaking off diplomatic relations with
any of the countries at war in Eu-
rere would rather spend a little money
on the army now," Mr. Mann continued,
“than to spend oceans of American
I think we ought to pre-

re for the worst now. .
Pe We are sitting on top of an
earthquake in the world. We are the
only great, rich, powerful country not
engaged in the war and the only one
without a method of defense. We may
become involved in war at any time
through our notions of the rights we
have or because of the cupidity of other
nations.

“I think we ought to remain at peace,
to stand even insult and injury, but
there is a limit beyond which no gne
goes. While in my. opinion we have hot
reached that limit, and while I hope we
shall be able to restrain ourselves so
that we shall never reach that limit, we
should prepare men to fight before we
pour out the blood of the volunteers,
unpr ed and untrained. An army of
250, men is not excessive. We should
be foolish not to provide it. When the
war clouds pass away we may reduce it,
but now we should prepare.”’

Representative Kahn, in urging the
— of the Senate amendment,
said:

“The time has come when the United
States should say to the world that we
are prepared to protect American life
and property in ‘every quarter of the
globe.’’ :

SEEK $250,000 FOR WELLS..

Ecstern Alumnae Begin Campaign
to Complete Endowment Fund.

More than 100 members of the Eastern
Association of the Wells College Alum-
nae met at Sherry’s yesterday for their
annual reunion and luncheon. The chief
object of interest among the friends of
the institution {s the raising of a half-
million-dollar endowment fund, toward
which the Rockefeller Foundation prom-
ises $100,000, provided $400,000 is raised
by June 16 ;

A report was made that $150,000 had
been pledged, and the Bastern Associa-
tion resolved on an energetic campaign
to obtain the remaining $250,000. For
that purpose a committee was appointed,
composed of Mrs. William Fellowes: Mor-
gan, Honorary Chairman; Miss Mary
Eustis, Acting Chairman; Mrs. Walter
Sullivan, Publicity Chairman; Miss Bess

the following as Captains: Mrs. Henry
Davenport, Miss Amelia Goodlatte, Mrs.
William Hasbrouck, Mrs. Richagd Hun-
ter, Mrs. Owen B. Huntsman, Miss Mar-
garet Moore, Miss Mildred Patterson,

Mrs. G. S. Tyson, and Mrs. Charles
Herrmann.

Mrs. Dion W. Kennedy, President of
the Bastern Association, presided, and
among the speakers were Dr. John H.

missioner; Edward S. Martin, and Dr.
Kerr D, Macmillan, President of. Wells
| College. Mr. Martin presented to Misa
Caroline Roe of the class of.1916 the
prize of $50 given annually by the East-
ern Association for the best English es-
say by an undergraduate. Miss Roe ts
the great-grandniece of the late E. P.
Roe. Mr. Martin was one of the judges.

“* One of the great needs of the hour is
to save paper,’’ he said. ‘‘ We write too
much, we print too much, we advertise
too much. What with war and our im-
mense addiction to print, the forests are
fast bea ge into the boilers of the
pulp mills and the price of paper. has

ve gloomy. It is a question with me
which does the most harm, newspapers
or rum. Being aware of the danger of
intoxicants, I have allowed my children

especially in, respect to paper: and ink,
and one result is that not one of them is
thus far addicted to the intoxicating ef-
fect of writing.’’
