HEARS STATEN ISLANDERS.

Mayor

Receives Committee with
Garbage. Plant. Protest.

Six residents of Staten Island who are
opposed to the establishment there of a
garbage reduction plant made their
complaint to Mayor Mitchel at the City
Hall yesterday. The committee pre-
sented the. Mayor with a copy of the pro-
test and resolutions passed at a mass
meeting last Thursday, and -after. the
conference went back to report to a
Vigilance Committee at a meeting to
be held on Staten Island last night.

.The committee said after the con-
ference that the Mayor had explainéd
in detail what led up to the present
attitude of the city, in selecting Staten
Island as the garbage disposal site, and
that the Mayor expressed his willing-
ness to work with the committee to
find a satisfactory solution of the prob.
lem, The committee made several sug-|
gestions to the Mayor, but it could not
be learned what they were. It was
said, however, that the suggestions

would be taken up for action by the
Vigilance Committee.

Mayor Mitchel explained that he told
the committee that he would be glad to
do what he could to help the peopk of
Staten Island. He said he had suggested
that a committee go to New Bedford
and examine the plant now in operation
there, but that his suggestion did not
seem to meet with favor.

The committee that waited on the
Mayor included the Right Rev. Mer. C.
A. Cassidy, rector of St. Peter’s Church,
New Brighton; Edward C. Bridgman,
President of the Staten Island Savings
Bank, Stapleton;. William S. Van Che,

and Robert T. Cone of: the-Civic League,

The marriage of Otto P. Heyn, son of
Mrs, O. P. Heyn of Staten Island, and
Miss Ethel Luise Just, daughter of Mr.
and Mrs. George A. Just of Scaredale,
N. Y., took place yesterday noon in the
Church of St, James-the-Less, Scars-
dale, the Rev. William O. Jarvis, the
rector, officiating. Pink roses with
Palms and smilax formed the decora-
tions.

The bride wore ivory white satin and
tulle with rose point, and carried
orchids and lilies. Miss Alice Van Horn,
the maid of honor, was in green taffeta
and silver lace, and carried American
Beauty roses. Miss Dorothy Just was
her sister's flower girl. William Ehler
Heyn was his brother’s best man, and
the ushers were George A. Just, Jr.,
F. A. Borgemeister, George O. Castell,
and Edwin Stumpp. The wedding break-
fast was served at Beaupel, the coun-
try home of the Justs.

-.Mr. Heyn is a son of the late Otto P.
Heyn, Vice President of William Stake|
& Co. He was graduated from Prince-
ton in 1912 and from the Columbia Law
School in 1915, and is a member of the
bar, Phi Beta Kappa, Phi Gamma
Delta, the Arch Club of Princeton, and

of Troop E. On their return from a

brief honeymoon they will live in New
York.

filed yesterday by Transfer Tax Ap-
praiser Charles Eweeney.

In the distribution of the estate Mrs.
Louise Harjes Moore, widow of the de-
cedent, received $795,151; Agnes Moore
Alaux, Millie Moore Caudoray, Louise
Moore and Hilda Moore, thé four daugh-
ters of the decedent, each received
passes to the decedent’s trustees for the
benefit of the widow and two brothers
of the decedent.

Affidavits submitted by Harry H.
Treadwell, Secretary and Assistant
Treasurer of Tifany & Co., were the
basis on which the valuation of the
stock was made. They showed that
the dividends for the years 1908, 1909
and 1910 were 25 per cent.; for 1911 they
were 85 per cent.; for 1912 and 1913 they
were 40 per cent; for 1914, 35 per cent.;
and for 1915, 25 per cent.

The highest known price paid for the
stock of Tiffany & Co., was $6,000 a
share when ten shares were bought by
the company itself in 1913. In 1914 one
share was sold for $5,700. There were
2,400 shares originally issued.

Mr. Treadwell’s affidavit of April 30,

DAVID H. KING’S WILL FILED.

Estate Divided Among Builder's
Daughters and Son.

The will of David H. King, Jr., who
laid the base of Liberty Statue and
built Madison Square Garden and many
other of the important buildings and
who died on April 20, was filed yesterday
for probate. Jeanne King, his daughter
living at 512 Fifth Avenue, is to re-
ceive an annuity of $5,000 and the de-
cedent’s automobiles and household ef-
fects. William Watson, 512 Fifth Av-

nition of services ‘‘in doing personal
work for me.’’

have had for some time. Thuse who

Sees No Place for It.
According to the credit manager of a
prominent lecal wholesale house, what-
ever advantages the so-called trade ac-
eeptance may have in other lines of
business there seems ta be no place for
it in the transactions between jobbers
and their customers. ‘*Take our house,
for instance,’’ he said. ‘‘ We have 10,-
or mere aceounts on our books, and
the credits run so small that $1,000
represents a heavy one. Quite a few of
the credits we carry do not exceed $100,
and there are many under.that amount.
To go in for trade acceptances with such
small ameunts would be a virtual revo-
lution in business methods, and I con-*
fess that I de not want to be the first
te da it. I believe that other-credit men
in the jobbing busineas fee] the same
way about it.

Holiday Hurts Cocoa Trade,

The celebration of the Easter holiday
in various Latin-American _ countries
caused’ a suspension of forward business
on raw cocoa in the last several days,
and spot business with buyers in_ this
country has been none too active. There
has been no real change in the export
situation as it affects shipments to Eu-
ropean countries, and the trade has
about given up hope of one for the bet-
ter until peace is declared. Despite the
quiet of the market and the fairly full
condition of stocks, prices hold up very
well. Those current yesterday showed
no great change for the worse when coni-
pared with quotations in force three
weeks ago. Some of the more important
prices fo low: Bahia, 15@16\4c. ; Caracas,
Maracaibo cocoa is held at 2(@21 cents a
pound.

Will Not Stop with_the Parade.

The Executive Committee of the silk
industries’ branch of the preparedness
enterprise does not intend to let its part
of the project die with the complétion
of the parade that is to be held here
on May 13. In a letter sent out to mem-
bers of the various branches of the silk
trade yesterday, William Skinner, Treas-
urer of the Siik Men’s Committee, says,
among other things: ‘‘ Your Executive
Committee does not expect to let this
good work stop with the parade. It will
endeavor to make use of the interest
manifested in the citizens’ preparedness
mévement by encouraging enrollment in
the citizens’ training camps and the
militia.’’ With the letter was Sent a list
of subscribers to the fund needed to de-
fray the expense incurred.in relation to
the parade. It showed that, up to April
P22, forty-eight individuals, firms, and
corporations had made contributions,

No ‘Cheeii to Decline in Rubber.
«Priceg.in the loeeal ‘market for crude
rubber continue to show the gradual
decline that has featured them for sev-

eral weeks past, and which is said to be
due to lack of buying interest on the
part of the larger users of this com-
modity. In spite of the steady easing
off there continues to be no ev ident sign
of selling pressure. Or, the other hand,
dealers are quick to raise prices when
the opportunity for a good sale is af-
forded. Practically all of the traders
in the market are wondering when
prices will again reach levels at which
big buyers will be interested, for no
hope of an immediate upturn is extended
by the condition of the English market.
Up-river fine was quoted yesterday at
71% cents, spot, while coarse was priced
at 55% cents. For spot and near-by de-
livery pale crepe was listed at 80 cents
and smoked sheets at a cent less. For
May-June délivery about half a cent a
pound lower could be done on both
grades,

DUTY ON SILK CRAPES.

Court of Customs Appeals Settles
a Test Case on it.

The United States Court of Customs
Appea}s has settled under the present
tariff ‘the classification of silk mourn-

ing crapes in the piece, varying in
width from 19 to 42 inches. The test
case stood in the name of Auffmordt &
Co., this city. The wide goods were
assessed for duty as veilings, while the
narrower. fabrics were taxed as trim-
mings, both at 60 per cent. -

Both classes of goods were claimed by
the importers to be dutiable at 45 per
cent. under the general provision for
woven fabrics of silk. The narrowér
widths of crape in question. are used
chiefly in making trimmings. In this
use the goods as imported are first cut
on a bias and then usually hemmed
and 5 ae to the garment, or it may
be a hat, the bias pieces being usually
folded and sewed together before being
applied. There axe also plaited crape
trimmi made from the samé mate-
rial, which in like manner had been cut
on thé bias and the pieces sewn to-
gether.

The Board of General Apprainors held
all the goods .to be trimmings dutiable
as assessed. The importers then went
before the Customs Court with the con-
tention at the goods were not trim-
mings, but cuatertal for trimmings, and
that the rule had ‘been established that
material for trimmings was not trim-
menee within the tariff sense. Presiding

Judge Montgomery, in his decision for
thé court, reversed the board and adopt-
ed the importers’ view.

overryjed the:/eontention and affirmed

Simon Brothers, San Francisco, pro-

was denied by the importers, who
claimed that the marking on the goods
was burnt in and not printed. Wudge
im affirmed the Collector.

under the provision for ‘‘ linseed,’’ call-

‘ uct.” .When. the issue came to trial it
was discovered that the merchandise in
the case had been assessed as.claimed by

was accerdingly averruled without af-

cent.

Altheugh the Customs Court in a ree
icent decision was understood to have

plants, the issue came up again yester-

‘ orchids,’’ while the importers claimed

was- decidedly impressive, representing

ment Talks of Payment.

The management of the American
Hide and Leather Conmipany issued a

statement to stockholders yesterday
which indicated that a dividend might

er be paid on the preferred stock after the |
next meeting of the board, in July. The

company paid 2 per cent. on its -pre-
ferred in 10905, but has paid nothing

since, and there is an unpaid accumula. |'

tion of about 113 per cent. in dividends

of the : ae ~ > pay y off the eee sae
mortg etore considering
ments on ee heey and thet whet, Pt 6
earnings for the year ending haope 80
are known the question of a disb
ment on the shares wil be considered.
Far ter agae yo wi added, however:

declaration should not be un- |-

derstood as necessarily implying that
the Directors are at the preseht time
committed to the payment of dividends
on the pret ferred. The published earn-
ings statements clearly indicate that the
profits: of the business in which the
company is engaged are subject to ex-
treme fluctuation. The large earnings

during the last eightee
resulted to a considerable extent om
the abnormal conditions brought about

by the Buropean war. How long present
conditions will continue is a question to
which no one can give a definite an-
swer. It is sible that at any. time
they may suddenly change in a manner
which would oe, affect earnings

even for the c

,000, against $852,000 a year ago and
$156,000 two years ago.

has enjoyed a large measure: of prosperity,
and for the calendar year 1915 practically
doubled its net- profits.

expansion in business? Are the earnings
likely to continue at the present.rate after
the war is over? These and other impor-
tant questions are answered in an analysis
of the property which we have just’ mailed
to our clients. ~

ttn |WEATHER © NEWS’. BEARISH

Liverpool Reports Tell of Further
Restricticn of Imports for Lack
of Bottoms to Carry It.

4o{ Although it may be too early to as-

sume that cotton has broken out of the
rut in which it has been moving for
such’ a long time, theré was'a notable

the fincrease yesterday in activity, and at

times the market displayed symptoms
‘of buoyancy. .The immediate influence
prométing activity ang strength was
the small amount of cotton delivered on
May. contracts. The volume of -notices
Was estimated at less than 2,000 bales.
It had been éxpected, héwever, that very
little ‘cotton would be, tendered, but as
soon as the impression was confirmed,
prices shot up rather sharply. The May
option opened-around 11.77, but before

jthe end of the second hour had sold as

high at 11.98. The close wag steady at
an advance of 5. to 7 points.

Otherwise, the news was rathér bear-
ish. The weathér was quite favorable,
although little or no rain was reported
in the Southwest.

Buying of May was\on a heavy scale
during. the forenoon.: . Purchases of this
option by half a dozen trade houses
were éstimated at trom 40,000 to 50;000,
while another broker brought about
10,000 bales of July.

A Liverpool cable dispatch says there
are strong indications of further restric-
tion in cotton imports owing to the di-
version of tonnage for the conveyance
of troops, munitions, and food. The
stock of cotton in Liverpool is consid-
ered fairly large, but the amount is not
sufficient to stand continued withdraw-
als for consumption without early re-
plenishment.

New Orleans showed a good deal of
strength during the day in apite of the
fact that deliveries in that mafket on
May contracts amounted to about 20,000
bales,

Call “ Check-off ” Un-American.

‘The operators maintain that the in-
sistence by the miners.on their demand
for a closed shop is un-American, and
that’ the forced collection of dues by the
employer, known as the * check-off,’ is
against the practice of every other
labor organization in .the country, and
is, in effect, a demand on, the part of the
officers and organizers of the United
Mine Workers of America for a guaran-
teed income, collected by the o ‘ators
and to be used by the organization in
any way it desircs. Much as they realize
the. responsibility of the step they take,
the operators beliéve that in rejecting
the demand for a closed.shop and the
“check-off’' they are protecting the in-
stitutions of the country as well as the
public without in any degree desiring to
antagonize the interests or the principles
of organized labor.

** This attitude on the part of the oper-
ators is in absolute accord with the de-
cision of see Anthracite Strike Commis-
sion Meg ed by the President of the
United States in 1902. On. this same sub-
ject of complete recognition of the union

thre’ commission found as follows:

‘The commission adjudges and
awards: That no person shall be refused
émploxyment or in any way discriminated
against on account of membership or
noen-membership.in any labor organizsa<-
tion, and that there shall be no diserini-
ination against or interference with any
employe who is not a member of any
labor organization by members .of such
organization.’ ’’

When shown the féregoing statement,
President White of the union declared
that the contention of the operators

N with reference to conditions in central

Pennsylvania did not harmonize with
the facts because the operators and
miners. of that district, known as Dis-

contract wherein the operators granted
the advance set forth in the New York
egreement.

Minor Points in Demands.

Aside from the three principal.. de-
mands, for an increase inthe -wage
rate, an eight-hour day, and a. complete
recognition of the union, the miners
wanted concessions on seven minor

points. Both sides. admitted that an
agreement could have been reached on
all of the minor propositions if the de-
mand for a closed shop and a “ check
off ’’ had been conceded.

In their answer to the demands of the
miners the operators at the opening of
the joint conference said that to grant
the demands would mean to eliminate all
profit from the mining industry. They
said that the 20 per cent. wage increase
alone which the miners demanded would
cost the companies $23,000,000 in four
years, and that this increase would raise
the oe of coal to the consumer and

LIGHT VOTE IN NEW JERSEY.

‘Wilson Delegates Chosen, Republi-
cans Are Unpledged. .

Special to The New York Times.

TRENTON, N. J., April 25.—Today’s
Presidential primaries in New. Jersey
were featured by a light vote and gen-
eral lack of interest. Unlike most elec-
tion nights, none of the State officials
Was at the Capitol this evening» and
none of the County Clerks arranged to
receive returns. |

There were no contests for the dele-
gates at large on either’ ticket. David
Baird of Camden, Newton A..K. Bug-
kg this city, Hamilton F. Kean of
Union County, and Ira Kip, Jr.,‘of Es-
sex, will go to the Republican National

nvention. Governor James F. Fielder,
United States Senator William Hughes,
State Purchasing Agent Edward E.
Grosscup, ‘and Representative Thomas
J. Scully constitute the Democratic “Big
Four.’’ The Republicans are unpledged,
but the Democrats all ran as Wilson
men and are bound to vote for his re-
nomination.

Interest in the election of alternate
delegates at large on the Republican
ticket centred in the candidacy of the
Rev. Dr. I. W. L. Roundtree, a negro

of this city. That he was defeated was
a foregone conclusion here late tonight.
The Democratic alternatea will be John-
ston Cornish, Robert D. te, William
A. Logue. and Richard Stockton, and the
Repudlicane will be C. Ledyard Blair,
Pierre P. Garven, Myron W. Robinson,
and Bloomfield H. Minch.

While the Republican ‘‘ Big Four ’’-is

unpledged, Mr. Bugbee has announced
his. opposition to Rooseyelt. The other
three are &nown to prefer some one else
than the Colonel, but are <a to

Living Costs 55.4 Per Cent.
Above the 1914 Levels

The National: Industrial Conference
Board, 10 East Thirty-ninth Street,
reported yesterday that the cost of
living among wage earners’ families
on June 15 last was 55.4 per cent.
higher than in July, 1914. But since
July, 1920, when. the peak of the rise
in the cost ofgliving since 1914 was
reached, price levels decreased 25
per cent., it was added.

Between May ‘15 and June 15 of
this year there was “a general in-
crease of threé-tenths of 1 per cent.
Clothing . prices dropped, which the
board thought was due to seasonal
variations, while food costs increased,

period apparently: balanced one an-

MORATORIUM SEEMS SURE

British and French Members of
Reparation Board Are Divided
on Duration of Relief.

By EDWIN L. JAMES,
Copyrisht, 1922, by The New York Times Company.
Special Cable to Tur New York TiMEs,
PARIS, July 20.—It is now certain
that some sort of moratorium on rep-
arations payments will be. granted to
Germany. The duration of this mora-
torium and the terms Germany will be
asked to accept in return for it will be
determined, probably next week, by the
Reparation Commission and then re-

viewed by the Allied Governments.

It is the idea of the French Govern-
ment that if Germany is aided by an
easing up on the part of the allies, Ger-
many should be induced or obliged to
make use of the improved situation to
put her fiscal affairs in order in a way
to assure the resumption of reparation
Payments on a sure scale.

The Committee on, Guarantees, which
has been for some weeks in Berlin
working out a methog for allied super-
vision of German. public ‘finances, re-

the Reparation Commission. teday that

lief sentiment among’ the members ts di-
vided. The English seem ‘to think that

Wadsworth and Calder Defend
and Vote For the “ Glovers-
ville "’ Schedule.

BILL MAY PASS IN AUGUST

Robinson Declares for Early Action
on Remaining Amendments
and Final Vote.

Special to The New York Times.

WASHINGTON, July 20.—By a ma-
jority of more than two to one the Sen-
ate, late this afternoon, administered a
severe rebuke to the Committee on
Finance when, by a vote of 38 to 17, it
refused to ratify the high duties the
committee had recommended for the
protection of the cotton glove industry.
Some of the duties proposed represented
ad valorem equiv@Ments of the specific
rates as high as 119 per cent.

An amendment proposed by Senator
Lenroot and adopted by the Senate pro-
vides that in no case shall the duty on
gloves of the kind covered by the sched- |
ule exceed 75 per cent. ad valorem. The |
revolting Republicans numbered twenty.

The repudiation of the committee foi- ;
lowed a debate that lasted more than |
four hours, the high duties proposed by |

the committee being defended by Sen-|
ators McCumber and Smoot and the New ;
York Senators, Wadsworth and Calder. |
This is the schedule popularly referred |
to as the ‘‘ Gloversville, New York,’’ |
schedule, because the principal advocate
for the rates was ex-Representative |
Littauer of Gloversville, one of the lead- |
ing figures in the American glove in-
dustry. The assault on the committee
was directed by Senators Lenroot and
Simmons.

Even Senator Lodge refused to vote
for the high duties proposed. He told
the Senate that in his opinion. they were
entirely too high. |

New York Senaters Defend Rates.

Senators Wadsworth and Calder de-
clared abate at . present the glovemakers
of Gloveraville were idle as a result.-of:
compétition from abroad and that jf the
factories were to be again operate at
full capacity the rates approved by the
committee were necessary.

‘*I dislike very much," said Senator
Lodge, ‘to disagree with the Committee
on Finance, but I have looked into this
matter and have been unable~to find
any comparison of the differences in
cost of production in this country and
abroad that would justify the imposition
of a duty as high as 119 per cent. ad
valorem. I think the amendment of the
Senator from: Wisconsin, which provides
a maximum duty of 75 per cent. ad
valorem, is ample."’

The ad valorem equivalents of the spe-
cific rates as proposed by the cammittee
began at 20 and 50 per cent. and then |
jumped to 84, 92 and 119 per cent., ac-
cording to the vaiue of the article.

FREE STATE GUNS |

BATTER WATERFORD

Heavy Bombardment of the City
Begun From Across the River
by Irish National Force.

20 ARE DEAD IN LIMERICK

Attack Developing. on Whole
Rebel Front—Government Re-
jects Compromise Peace.

Copyricht, 1922, by The New York Times Company.
Special Cable to TH» New York TIMES,

DUBLIN, July 20 (Passed by Military
Censor).—A few days ago the boast was
made on the irregulars’ behalf that de
Valera was with’ the Director of Oper-
ations in Limerick, but now irregular
headquarters are transferred to some
safer spot. Doubtless the capture of
Limerick is in sight and it means the
collapse of the citadel/ which the irreg-
ulars had persuaded themselves ren-
dered their left flank impregnable and
defied any possibility of a successful
turning movement against their main
positions. But the guns have opened. on
Waterford, rendering the right wing's
position. extremely critical.

Today. Waterford City is the great
military objective. National troops ‘are
bombarding it vigorously. Machine guns
send messages of death over the waters
of-the River Suir. The broad and rap-
idly flowing tidal river with its famous
tcll bridge prevents the troops for the
moment from coming-into close :
with the ¢r¥régulars. ane

The attack began at 7 o'clock on Tues-
day evening when the almost deserted
eity awoke to thé cracking of rifles and
rattling of machine .guns heralding the
bursting war cloud overhanging it three
weeks. The national forces from Kil-
kenny under command of Col. Com-
mandant Prout who laid siege to the
city and coulda have entered it twenty-
four hours ago but for the raising of
the drawbridge between the city proper
and the.majn roads and railways emerg-
ing from the Kilkenny side of the river.
The ferry ‘bark district and all the
north bank of the river facing the city
are in the hand of nationals who from
concealed positions in the ‘woods of
Mount Misery rising over the railway
terminus rain showers of lead on the
irregulars’ positions along the quay from
the hotel opposite the drawbridge to
Reginald’s tower, that dark old castle
dating back to Danish times.

It is a great military operation, and a
splendid prelude to certain and final
restoration of the whole of the southern
province to the poople whose overwhelm-
ing verdict established their right at
the election.

On the march from Kilkenny the
troops bivouacked ‘in the meadows of
Kilmacow, and before resumption re-
ceived: general absolution from’ Father
Greene. The picture of the men with
Colonel Prout.at their head kneeling
en masse before the vested priest is not
easily forgotten.

Waterford’s inhabitants have fled for
the moment, while deliverence of the
city is being secured, though at frightful
cost of shrapnel and high explosive
shells.

Special to The New York Times.
WASHINGTON, July 20.—Hope that |
the way might be cleared for immediate
settlement of the railway strike was |

dashed to the ground soon after mid- |

Kelfogg and Watson of the Senate: In-
terstate Commerce Committee emerged
from a conference with five of the prin-
cipal Eastern railway executives whom
they had asked to come to Washington
for a free and frank discussion of the|
situation.

Besides the Senators named the con-|
ference was participated in by Thomas}
De Witt Cuyler of Philadelphia; a di-|
rector of the Pennsylvania system and |
Chairman of the Railway Executive |
Committee; L. F, Loree of New York,
President of the Delaware & Hudson;
Wiliam W. Atterbury of Philadelphia,
Vice President of the Pennsylvania
system; E. J. Pearson of the New. York,
New Hayen & Hartford linea and Frank
Hy Alfred. of the Pere Marquette sys-
tem, om,

present. f
The raf! heads who were summoned
to Washington by the spokesmen for the |
Senate Interstate Commerce Committee
arrived just before 9 o’clock, went at
once to a hotel, were closeted with the
three Senators until midnight and im-
mediately after the conference all but
Messrs. Cuyler and Thom hurried to the |
Union Station and teok trains back to |
New York and Philadelphia.
None of the railway executives would |
discuss the conference. On their dae-
parture from the hotel they said: that
Senator Cummins would have something
to say.
Statement by Cummins.

Soon after midnight this statement
was issued by Senator Cummins:
‘“‘Senators Kellogg, Watson and my-
self had a conference with some of the
Eastern railroad Presidents this eve-
ning for the purpose of talking over
the strike situation and of ascertaining,
if possible, the exact issues between the
roads and the strikers.

‘““We wanted to discover whether
there is any explanation that would re- |

move the difficulties in the way of an
adjustment.

*““We discussed the whole
freely and frankly.

““The views of the shopmen have al-
ready been fully disclosed at Chicago.

““The object of the conference was
solely to secure information upon this!
very vital subject.’’

Senator Cummins could not be per-
suaded, by questioning to add to the}
statement. He would not discuss the
details. of the conference. Nor would
he discuss future developments.

Despite the reticence of Senator Cum-
mins and others participating in the con-
ference it was ascertained that no -real
headway was made toward an adjust-
“ment. One of the Senators present,
however, without allowing his name to
be used, said:

‘“All I-care to say is that it is a
damned serious situation.’’

The conference came as a surprise to
the few in Washington who were first
advised of it in dispatches from New
York, saying that a delegation of Hast-
ern rail executives was coming to Wash-
ington. for a midnight conference with
Chairman Cummins and other members
of the Senate Finance Committee.

situation

Senators Reflect Failure.

It was learned from one of the partici-
pants in the conference that’ the free
and frank discussion held open no pros-
pect for immediate settlement, and the
failure of the conference was reflected
in the countenances of the Senators who
participated.

Prior to the break-up of the meeting. {
which had been hurriedly called, hope
had existed in Administration circles
that means might be found for a prompt
settlement. During the last twenty-
four’ hours the belief had been growing
that some kind of an adjustment of the
rail strike was imminent.

it was’ the hope of -the Senatorial

might be removed by legislation satis-
faciory .to: the rail heads and strike
leaders. But. this idea vanished after
the Senators went into the situation
with the rail. heads.

Senator Cummins has.-been in touch
with. President Harding almost . daily
relative to the railway situation. He
will acquaint the President with latest
developments: in tonight's conference,

The President has been reluctant to
intervene in:the rail strike, holding that
thé Railroad Labor Board, as the Fed-
eral agency authorized by law to deal
with ‘the situation was the logical Gov-

TOPEKA, Kan., July 20.—Governor
Henry J. Allen tonight authorized the |
arrest of William White, editor of. the |
Emporia Gazette, for alleged. violations
of the anti-picketing proviston of the |

|Kansas Industrial Court.

The Governor issued a long statement |
on the subject. In it he says that after |
the shopmen's strike began, the strikers
tried various methods of picketing, only
to have these declared violations of the
law. Then he relates how: finally the |
strike leaders provided themselves with
cards containing a declaration of sym-
pathy for the strikers and induced mer- j
ehants in two or three shop towns toe put)
these in their windows.

This the Attorney-General held to be
another violation of the law. . Most
merchants, on request, says the Gov- |
ernor, removed these cards and no.ar-
rests were ordered.

The statement goes on:

‘‘ William Allen White, of Emporia,
who has: been one of the strike sym-
pathizers from the beginning, is the
first man to openly defy the law offi-
cers in this matter and to declare his
intention to display the slogan of the
strike leaders in his shop window and
to continue this form of encourage-
ment to the men who are now’ violat-
ing the law of the State.

‘“*Mr. White is a man with a poten-
tial following in the State, and his
declaration that he. did not intend to
@bey this law has aroused a sympa-
thetic response among. other strike
Sympathizers. Cards that were taken
down yesterday in. obedience to the
request of law. officers are being put
the result. of Mr.
White’s action, and a new spirit of
hostility and determination has been
aroused in the minds of the strikers,
who believe that in Mr. White they
have secured a champion whose ex-
ample will justify them in new ‘acts
of disobedience to the law. ~

going to be able to stop this, practice
in Kansas without arrests and prose- |
cutions. No distinctions will be. made
as to individuais, no: matter what. their
standing may be'in the State .or nation

ig @ simple concrete question. as _ to

CLEVELAND FACING DARKNESS.

Days, Says Director.

CLEVELAND, July 20.—Cleveland's
municipal light plant will be forced to
shut down within three days and 32,000
|consumers will be deprived of electric
eurrent unless the city’s coal supply is
replenished within that time, the Public
Utilities Director, Mr. Roberts, declared
|} today. ‘
| The plant has only three days’ supply
of coal on hand and all hope of oper-
ating its generators with natural gas
fuel has been abandoned, he said.

Special to The New York Times.

LANSING, Mich., July 20.—Governor
Alex J. Groesbeck met with his first set-
back today in his plan to open the coal
mines in the Saginaw district and oper-
ate them as State institutions.

Following a conference in Saginaw
yesterday with miners and mine owners,
ithe Governor announced that he was
prepared to, take over and operate the
coal mines for the good of the public.
Today John L.~Lewis, President of the
United Mine Workefs, wired the Gover-
nor from Washington that if the State
desired to operate the coal mines the
Governor also would have to make terms
with the mine employes now on a strike
before opening the mines.

This was taken to mean that the min-
ers would not go back to work even
though the State did take over the oper-
ation of the mines. The question is to
be taken up this week with the mine
workers’ officials. The Governor de-
clares the mines must be worked.

SQUAD AWES TROLLEYMEN.

Minor Outbreaks Occur

State Troopers Arrive.

BUFFALO, N. Y., July 20.—While
State troopers were being rushed into
Buffalo from four of the six headqumr-
ters of the State Constabularv. the
International Railway Company was
preparing tonight to extend service on
its trolley lines tied up for nineteen days
by the strike of motormen, conductors
and barnmen.,

No serious trouble occurred today, the
appearance of the city police riot squad
with sawed-off shotguns and the ap-
proach of the State poliee apparently
putting fear into the hearts of the dis-
orderly element that led the east side
rioting for two days.

Several minor outbreaks occurred
while the limited number of cars were
making last trips for the day on the
east side lines about 6 o clock this eve-
ning. A car was derailed at Seneca and
Spring Streets and the crew was stoned.
Other cars were bombarded on Walden
Avenue and Genesce Street, the scene of
vesterday’s disorders.

A few State troopers reached the out-
| skirts of the eclty late this afternoon,
but did not go on patrol duty. They
will be housed at a State armory. Major

Ohio Troops Sent Into Field.

COLUMBUS, Ohio, July 20 (Associated
Press).—Governor Davis late today
ordered National Guard troops now
mobilized to proceed immediately into
the coal mining districts, and also
ordered additional units mobilized.

Three infantry companies, one machine

fun company and one motor transport
company began entraining immediately
for Cadiz, Harrison County, for duty in
the Fastern coal fields. Another com-
pany of infantry at Lancaster will be
held in readiness for, operation in the
Southern fields.

A survey of the coal. situation in
Brooklyn by Samuel Drummond, secre-
tary of the Brooklyn Coa] Exchange,
made public yesterday by the Brooklyn
;Chamber of Commerce, said that the
| fuel shortage was already apparent, and
a severe Winter would
siderable suffering.’’

‘If mining is resumed within the next
week," he added, ‘*‘ the mines worked to
capacity, and we have a comparatively
mild Winter, it is probable we will get
through without suffering, mainly be-
cause, last Winter being an open one,
there were about 8,000,000 tons of do-
mestic sizes of anthracite on hand at
the mines, in transit and in retail deal-
ers’ yards when the suspension became
effective on April 1. It must be re-
membered, however, that over three
months idleness means a loss of produc-
tion of all sizes of anthracite of about
20,000,000 tons, and this loss cannot pos-
sibly be made up.”’

McClellan & Junkersfeld, Inc., ‘engi-
neers for the Union Electric Light &
Power Company, announced their de-
cision to burn powdered coal] in the new
$6,000,000 power plant this company is
building in St. Louts.

Declaring this one of the most impor-
tant forward steps in engineering, they
said that ‘‘ extensive tests and investi-
gation by the engineers on stoker equip-
ment and pulverized fuel equipment
proved that coal in powdered form was
a most desirable fuel, giving more eco-
nomical results than any other type of
combustion equipment and permitting
the use of mining sweepings, low grade
and non-marketable coals, which are
often wasted.

‘‘The burning of powdered coal is as
simple as the burning of fuel oil,’’ it
was stated, ‘‘ and hag many of the ad-
vantages of this fuel, and in an emer-
gency due to miners’ strikes, or other
unforeseen causes, fuel oll may be used
in the same furnaces without change.

BATTER WATERFORD

DUBLIN, July 20 (Associated Press).—
Reports from the fighting area received
today indicate a pressure by the national
army forces on each extremity of the
insurgent line, developing powerfully
and extending roughly from Limerick to

Waterford, thereby cutting off practi-
cally the whole of Munster Province.

At Limerick fighting was progressing
last evening. The National troops
launched a heavy attack with bombs on
the O’Mara factory, but as far as is
known the irregulars are still holding the
position. In the centre of the city; where
the insurgents are strongly fortified, the
firing was particularly heavy. The cas-
ualties are estimated at twenty. killed
and forty wounded, a considerable por-
tion of these being civilians.

BELFAST, July 20 (Associated Press).
—The Irish Army bulletin for this after-
nooh says that it is reported the irregu-
lars retreated from Tullamore at 4
o'clock this morning after burning the
barracks, the courthouse and the jail.

They left in several lorries in different
directions. A

Alarming accounts of the situation in
Kings County, or County Offaly, as it is
now known, reached Belfast in dis-
patches received today. Tullamore and
Birr are described as in a pitiable plight
with those of their inhabitants who are
able to do so taking flight in fear of
starvation.

One party which volunteered to go
from Tullamore to some of the outlying
villages to procure food and milk for
the women and children was held up by
the Republicans on the way back, the
messages state, and the supplies com-
mandeered.

A new order has been issued at
Tullamore that any motor car arriving
in the town must be kept for military
purposes, and according to The Belfast
Telegraph correspondent all males from
fourteen years upward in the region
between Tullamore and Birr are being
conscripted. A large section of the con-
scripts, however, is reported to have de-
serted and joined the national forces,
some of them arriving in the neighbor-
ing villages wearing only their trousers
and shirts, having left their various
barracks during the night.

Dublin -wag again isolated from Bel-
fast today, both as regards railroad and
|} telephonic communications.

D. C. COLLIER EXONERATED.

Commissioner to Brazil Fair Freed
of Harrison Charges.

Special to The New York Times.

WASHINGTON, July 20.—The complete
exoneration of D. C. Collier, Commis-
sioner General of the United States to
theBrazilian Centennial Exposition, from
charges made by Frank A. Harrison of
Nebraska, whose resignation from the
commission was accepted by President
| Harding after his removal had been de-
manded by his fellow Commissioners,

by the State De-
partment after a detailed inquiry lasting
several weeks.

Ice on the Shares
of the Arabian Sea

A wonderfully interesting letter
tells Knickerbocker about ice
in Cochin, on the coast of sun-
baked India: “In the club at

ochin, when you get a cool drink
you sign a chit for the drink and on
the chit is an item for the few tiny
crumbs of ice that _ the liquid a
faint refreshing chill. One afternoon
i wasin the spacious dnd really mag- .
nificent old house of one of the -
Englishmen. Lemonade was
around and the lady of the house
followed up the servant and fished
up from the depths of a wide-
mouthed thermos bottle a bit of ice
apiece. She apologized for the tiny
ration of ice. telling us that the
supply had not come over from Mad-
ras that day and until it came we
should have to put up with what
ice was left.”
Mr. George Rouschline, Knickerbocker’s
expert on Scientific Ice Plants, built the
first successful commercial Ice Plant in.
India. The plant is located at Calcutta...

STATE TROOPS OUT
AT CONCORD, N. H.

Governor Acts Following the
Attack on Rail Workers—
East Deerfield Man Shot.

GEN. EDWARDS IN TOUCH

Reports Disorders to Washington,
Stops Federal Troops’ Leave and
Confers With Governor.

CONCORD, N. H., July 20.—A detach-
ment of artillerymen, sixty strong, in
charge of Captain Arthur L. Smith, ar-
rived here from Portsmouth at 10
o'clock tonight in response to Governor
Brown's order late today calling out
State troops to protect railroad property
and workers here. The station was al-
most deserted when the troop train
pulled in,

The men marched immediately to the
Boston & Maine Railroad yards, where
they will be quartered. ;

Harley C. Brown, an employe of: the
Boston & Maine Railroad, reported to
the: police that he had been taken from
an electric car by about twenty. men
late today, and beaten with fists; and
clubs. He exhibited severe bruises.

Officials of the Federated Shop Crafts
today urged members of the union or-
ganizations who are special officers of
the police force to tender their services
to the City Marshal for police duty
during the present strike situation.

Strikers Deny Responsibility.

BOSTON, July 20.—Mobilization of
two companies of the New Hampshire
National Guard for strike duty at Con-
cord and the shooting of a Boston &
Maine machinist’s helper near Hast
Deerfield were leading events in the
railroad situation in New England to-
day,

Governor Albert O. Brown of New
Hampshire directed the calling out of the
troops in the State capital following a
conference at Manchester with Adjutant
General Howard, at which the request

of Mayor Henry Chamberlin of Concord
for protection was considered. The

Mayor, in a letter to the Governor, said
that in his opinion the police force was
“insufficient to afford the protection
now required if the authority of the law
is to be maintained and anything like
normal railroad service is to be con-
tinued.”’

Rioting in Worcester.

WORCESTER, Mass., July 20.—Riot-
ing and violence in the railroad yards in
Worcester developed to such a magni-
tude during the night that extra police
guards were detailed to the various
| railroad properties here.

The Boston & Maine Railroad was
made to bear the brunt of the trouble,
and men hired to take the places of
striking shopmen, stationary “engineers
and oilers were stoned, and freight
trains held up for hours by the slashing
of airbrake hose.

Four Shot in Pennsylvania.

MONONGAHELA, Pa., July 20.—Two
Pennsylvania Railroad patrolmen, a car
inspector and a constable were shot
early today after their gasoline speed-
ster had been wrecked on the Ellsworth

branch, south of Bentleyville, Pa. Three
of the men were seriously wounded,
while the other was hit by a number of
buckshot. The officers were On railroad
strike patrol duty.

The rail executives were sald tq have

self, and that apparently any further
moves must come through the Railroad
Labor Board, the railroad executives or
the union representatives. One of the
conferees said that. the future part of
the Government now appeared to be the
task of maintaining. order on the strike-
affected rail lines and at the same time
in the coal fields.

RAIL BOARD IS UPHELD
AGAINST PENNSYLVANIA

Federal C enit Réleerses Order Re-
straining Criticism of Road
for Ignoring Decision.

Special to The New York Times

CHICAGO, July 20.—The claim of the
Railroad Labor Board to possess the
power of criticising those who ignore
its decisions appeared to be upheld to-
day in a judgment rendered by Justices
Baker, Altschuler and Evans in the Fed-
eral Court of Appeals, reversing the de-
cision of Federal Judge Page in the
test case of the Pennsylvania Road in
connection with a decision of the board.

The decision, in effect, not only re-
stores props that had been knocked from
under the labor unions, but it removes
a grievance that railway shopmen have
nursed for months.

In a controversy between the board
and the Pennsylvania Railroad, Judge
Page had ruled that the board was not
an integral part of the Government, was
a corporate body, and therefore could
sue and be sued.

The decision has an important bearing
on the present railroad strike inasmuch

as the original dispute involved the
forming of a ‘* company union ”’. by the
Pennsylyania, which refused to meet
unions of the federated shop crafts.
The railroad insisted that it had the
right to deal with its own employes and
Judge Landis supported this contention
by granting a_ temporary injunction
restraining the Labor Board from criti-
cising the actions of the railroad in con-
nection with the company union matter.
Later Judge Page made the injunction
permanent.

In his decision Judge Page ruled that
the Railroad Labor Board had exceeded
its authority and had jurisdiction only
in cases directly concerning wages and
working rules. :

The decision was appealed by Solicitor
General Beck, who contended that it
would invalidate hundreds of the board's
rulings. Today’s action of the Court
of Appeals, it was predicted, will invali-
date the wage agreement which the
Pennsylvania Railroad recently an-
nounced it had made with its shop em-
ployes, because the Labor Board found
that the road was dealing with repre-
sentatives of less than 15 per cent. of
its employes, without considering the
sentiments of the remainder of the
workers. Officials of the road this week
announced that the new wage agree-
ments affected 14 ),000.

Reversal of Judge Page’s rulings Is
held to mean that the Pennsylvania,
the most prominent carrier fostering
the open shop, will be compelled to meet
with shop crafts representatives in se-
lecting employes to méet with its of-
ficials.

Promoters of peace in the railway
strike, recovering from +» Wednesday
night’s announcement that all negotla-
tions here’ were at an end, gained new
hope today from an. overture by the
Baltimore & Ohio Railway.

Cc, Galloway, Vice President of
the road, announced that since the
peace movement undertaken by Ben W.
Hooper, Chairman of .the board, had
failed, the company is*~‘‘ now ready to
econfér with its men ”’ on the question of
settlement.

Superintendents over the entire system
were instructed promptly to notify the
men that the company desires to deal
with them.

Denison Labor Leader’s Charges.

DENISON, Texas, July 20.—Charges
that railroads are purposely delaying
the mails in an effort to bring about
the calling out of Federal troops were
made today by E. M. Wilson, Chatrman
of the Federated Shop Crafts on the
Missouri, Kansas & Texas Railroad. In
a statement given out here Mr. Wilson
asserted that mail and express trains
are being sidetracked for less important
trains so they will be delayed.

ST. LOUIS, Mo., July 20.—Deniai of
charges made at Denison by E, H. Wil-
son that the railroads are delaying the
mails in an effort to bring out Federal
troops was made at the general offices
of the Missouri, Kansas & Texas Rail-
road late today.

The statement declared that the road
was running its trains ‘‘as fast and as
closely on schedule as possible."’

Wabash Cancels Six Trains.

CINCINNATI, Ohio, July 20.—Superin-
tendent R. N. Bird of the Government
mail service announced here today that
the Wabash Railroad has taken off six
‘‘important trains,'’ due to the railroad
and coal strikes, and that it would ‘‘con-
siderably slow up the mail service in
this division.”’

The trains annulled, according to Su-
perintendent Bird, are Train 9,  be-
tween Detroit and St. Louis, Trains 18
and 28, between St. Louis and Detroit;
Train 19, between Toledo and Fort
Wayne; Train 18, between Fort Wayne
and Toledo, and Train 6, between St.
Louls and Decatur, Ill.

ST. LOUIS, Mo., July 20.—Denial that
discontinuance of six trains would inter-
fere greatly with the movement of mails
was made this afternoon by E. J. Taus-
sig, President of the Wabash Railroad,
Mr. Taussig asserted that the Wabash
was operating more trains at present
than when under Federal control, and
that. the annuliment of six tyaihs was
due to lack of passenger travel.

CLERKS ON TWO ROADS OUT,

Strike Is Expected to Slow Up
Southern Coal Shipments.

CINCINNATI, Ohio, July 20.—E. H.
Fitzgerald, Grand President of the
Brotherhood of Railway and Steamship

Clerks, Freight Handlers, Station and |

Express Employes, said that unofficial
reports reaching his office indicated
that the strike on Western railroads
called for 10 A. M. today on the Chesa-
peake & Ohio and Norfolk was 100 per
cent. effective at many points,

After a personal canvass of the Cin-
cinnati terminal today Mr. Fitzgerald
said that 327 freight handlers and clerks
here had walked out.

With clerks, freight handlers and sta-
tion men going on strike, union officials
here today predicted a further tighten-
ing up of the available supply of coal
of the nation.

BUSINESS MEN ARE AROUSED

Americans Who Are Opening Up
bh New Markets Fear Defeat if

Copyright, 1922, by The New York Times Company.
Special Cable to Tue New York TiMEs,

CAIRO, July 20.—Everybody in Egypt
With the faintest idea of economics—
Americans, British, French, Italians,
Greeks, Egyptians and the real polyglot
community—is watching. anxiously the
‘trend of American policy concerning the
import duty on long staple cotton into
the United States.. The matter is one of
national importance to Egypt, and in a

pveeeet degree to America. 2

. During this week international cap-
tains of commerce in Cairo and Alexan-
dria were interviewed on this _matter.
‘_In the main their views are identical.
American business men, with close
knowledge of cotton-growing conditions
in the United States, point out that if
. the present temporary import duty on
long ‘staple cotton into the United States
is incorporated permanently in the new
tariff legislation it will constitute the

thin. end of the wedge which ultimately
will split Egypto-American commercial
relations asunder. They point out -that
the fundamental fact in the case ts not
the protection needed for long staple
cotton grown in the United States, but
that the American grown long staple
is inferior to Egyptian long staple and
canrot replace Egyptian in American
manufacturing industries. They say fur-
ther that protection of long staple must
have as an inevitable corollary a pro-
tective tariff. for short staple cotton.
This means American industries wiil be
forced to use inferior cotton, notably for
tires. Thus, while thousands of farmers,
perhaps, will gain a slight advantage
through the tariff, millions of farmers
and business men generally~ in, the
United States will suffer disadvantage
through having to use automobile tires
and other cotton products which neces-
sarily.are inferior in quality to those at
present in use. Or, if long staple cotton
is prohibitively taxed while long staple
products are allowed to enter the United
States practically on a free trade basis,
the American tire industry, for instance,
is bound to be badly hit. ;

However, even if the reaction ‘in the
United States were not serious, there
are other important considerations re-
quiring careful attention. It is neces-
sary to recognize that the import duty
on Egyptian cotton eventually means
the elimination of Egyptian cotton from
American industry. This indeed is the
aim of the American cotton growers who
are urging that the duty be made-per-
manent.

if the duty is confirmed the first_ef-
fect on American foreign commerce wil!
be the loss of Egypt's trade with
America. Last year this amounted -to
$50,000,000. Thus at a stroke of the
pen American legislators will lose for
America more than $50,000,000 annually
just at a time when American business
men now in Egypt are developing grow-
ing markets for American manufactures.
if America bars out [Egyptian cotton,
Egypt obviously will be seriously impov-
erished and American commercial pio-
neers in Egypt will have to retreat fur-
ther.

If Egyptian cotton is unable to enter
the United States there will be a sub-
stantia] loss to the United States Ship-
ping Board, whose ships now find prof-
{table cargoes in the transporting of
Egyptian cotton to American ports.
Otherwise they would be empty on the
homeward journeys.

It is estimated here that if tariff legis-
lation drives Egyptian cotton from
America the total loss to the United
States will be more than $100,000,000
annually.

Finally there is another aspect. Amer-
fica having capitulations in Egypt is safe
from retaliation. If-America makes the
prohibitive tariff on Egyptian cotton
permanent it is tantamount to tying an
opponent's hands, then ‘hitting him in
the face.

In the foregoing only such arguments
ere given as are presented by American
business men here who are willing to
“repeat them to any American authority.
Other nationalities in business ~ in
Egypt ‘go even further in their state-
ments.

IN JACKSON'S LUNGS

Physician’s Testimony Protested
by Counsel for Exterminator, on
Trial for Manslaughter.

Despite objections by counsel for Al-
bert Bradicich, a vermin exterminator,
who is being tried for manslaughter on
the charge of causing the deaths of. Mr.
and Mrs. Freemont M. Jackson in their
apartment in the Hotel Margaret Annex
in Brooklyn last April/ the: prosecution
got before the jury yesterday testimony
to show that cyanogen gas in the lungs
was detected at the autopsy.

It was charged that Bradicich was
careless in releasing. cyanogen gas in
an apartment below the Jackson’s and
that the gas seeped through crevices
in the floor and overcame:.them. Dr.
William W. Hala, who assisted in the
autopsy° on Mr. Jackson's. body, said
that when he opened the chest cavity
he distinctly smelled the gas and spoke
of it to Dr. Charles Wuest, the medical
examiner.

**I told Dr. Wuest,”’ he said, “that
I believed Mr. Jackson -had died of cy-
anogen poisoning because of, the odor
from his Jungs, after which Dr. Wuest
left..the room.”

County Judge Haskell told the jury
that they should not consider Dr. Hala’s
testimony that of an expert, inasmuch

as he had never treated a case of cy-
anogen gas poisoning.

LEGAL RUM SUPPLY
HALVED THIS YEAR

Total Withdrawals From Govern-
ment Warehouses Estimated at

The ‘volume of liquor legaHy with-
drawn from Government warehouses
during 1922 will be a little more than
|half of that taken out’ in 1931 and less

than a sixth of that issued in 1920, ac-
cording to an estimate given out yester-
day by Federal Prohibition. Commis-
sioner Roy A. Haynes, who visited New
York prohibition, headquarters, at 1,107
Broadway,, yesterday. ;

‘In 1920 there were legally withdrawn
from Government waréhouses and other
sources 12,000,000 gallons of: good, ‘or
red, liquor. The figures for 1921 were
3,500,000, while our estimate of the total
withdrawals for this year, based on
those of the first-quarter, 1s 1,s00,000

“There is little qyestion, but that 50
per cent. of the improvement in general
prohibition —- throughout the
country is due to
bootleg market with inferior liquor. As
the withdrawals of good«liquor have
been decreased, poor grade ,and often
poisonous substitutes have been resorted
to, so that many persons who in the
past occasionally used liquor. refrain
now from drinking on account of fear of
being poisoned.”

SEA PIRATES KILL SKIPPER.

Men in Motor Boat Board Schooner
and Shoot Her Master.

MIAMI, Fla., July 20.—The converted
| auxiliary schooner, Willam H. Albury
was held up by motor-boat pirates off
Gun Key today and her master, Captain
Edgecombe, shot. dead on deck, accord-
ing to a wireless message from Bimini
picked up by the Miami Beach Radio
Station tonight.

The message said the Albury was held
up by men in a motorboat bearing the
name Falcon and the license number
V-7456. The Falcon escaped and the
Albury headed for Bimini, where the

body of the captain was taken off.

“In comparison with its (the Norris
}Plan’s) provision regarding fertilizer,
| the. Ford offer sinks into absolute in-

WITH WAR FRAUDS

Attorney General Organizes
Special Division to Decide Dis-
position of Every Case.

GIVES BODY FULL POWERS

Daugherty Himself Barred. From
Dropping Any Suit Without.the
Board’s Authorization.

Special to The New York Times.

WASHINGTON, July 20.—Final de-
cision for prosecuting or dropping war
contract cases will rest with a special
board of review and not with any one
person in the Department of Justice, it
Was announced today in a department
@tatement outlining the organization of

the special division authorized by a
$500,000 Congressional appropriation to
investigate war fraud cases,

So broad are the powers of this special
board that not even Attorney General
Daugherty can drop a war contract suit
without its authorization. This announce-
ment indicates a departure from the
original plan organizing the special De-
partment of Justice division for prosecu-
tion of war fraud cases, when Mr.
Daugherty declared that final decision
as to what suits should be brought and
what cases dropped would rest with him,
and him alons.

The new body will be known as the
Board of Administration and Review
and will be composed of the Attorney
General, six of his assistants and others
whom he may desire to appoint.

It was noted in the statement that
the new division authorized by

1ess, which is now pusving the surplus
umber cases and investigation of the
Chemical Foundation before the Dis-
trict of Columbia Grana Jury, is of-
fictally known as the War Transactions
Section, rather than~ by its previous
designation of War Frauds Section.

The appointment of an advisory
couneil to render opinions upon pro-
ceedure and points of law in war con-
tract cases also was announced. This
body will be composed of former Sena-
tor Charles S. Thomas of Colorado,
former Judge T. H. Bigger of Columbus,
Ohio, and Charles Ferr, recently re-
signed as United States Judge of the
Panama Canal Zone.

The Department of Justice statement
gays, in part:

‘*The new section has been
Attorney General Daugherty has
ney General as counsel-in-charge.

in the future to such other sub-divisions |

to time the expert legal assistance es- |

sential to the prosecution of the various
cases coming under them,

‘“‘ As the head of the board of admin-
istration and review and of the advisory
council, the Attorney General is in a po-
sition to be at all times in
control of the legal work of the depart-
ment growing out of the war cases, and

to be in constant toucn with all develop- |

ments, but the system kas been so de-

vised that every decision with respect to!

or with!
respect to dropping cases where the out- |

the prosecution of a criminal case,
the bringing of a civil suit,

look is not favorable, must be taken,
not by any individual in the department,

including the Attorney General himself, |

of the best legal talent the Government
has been able to obtain.

*“ Miscellaneous cases referred by the |

ceil, are to be carefully considered and
@ written report and recommendation
will be made to the Attorney General
in each case. In cases where prosecu-

“Under the instructions of Attorney
General Daugherty, when a case has
been assigned to counsel such counsel
shall: have and exercise full authority
and control over all proceedings thereon
and will be held responsible for the

reparation and presentation of the case
n all its phases. Except. in cases of

the counsel assigned to the case are re-

Provides for Dissenting Opinions.

‘An important provision of the plan
under which the war contract cases are
being prosecuted by the Government is
that any member of the Board of Ad-
ministration and Review shall have the
rig::t ts have his dissenting vote on any
questioa made a matter of record and
to file dissenting opinion in any matter
which has been passed on by the board.
Thus the utmost freedom of action is
given to the board and its members, and
no action can be taken without the rea-
|sons for that action becoming a matter
of public record. ;

‘““An administrative officer has been
designated to have charge of the carry-
ing out of all administration matters
relating to the War Transactions Sec-
tion and of its proper co-ordination with
the other divisions of the Department of
Justice through the Assistant Attorney
General in charge of administration.’’

The statement says that the War
Transactions Section has been divided
into five subdivisions, which will have
charge of cases growing out of contracts
concerning aviation, camps and canton-
ments, Quartermaster Corps, ordnance
and foreign expenditures and miscella-
neous cases.

NO VOTING MACHINES
| TO BE SET UP HERE

|Makers Are Unwilling to Face
Litigation Certain to Follow
Their Installation.

ALBANY, N. Y., July 20.—No voting
machines will be installed in New York
City this Fall, Secretary of State John
J. Lyons announced this afternoon. The
| reason given was that the only company
| manufacturing machines ‘‘that have
j} stood the test of time, and which ‘is
| equipped to the extent of being able to
supply New York with the required num-
| ber of machines this Fall, has come to
the decision that it does not want to
enter into any contract, so far as New
York City is concerned.’’

The law authorizes the Secretary of
State to let the contract for enough ma-
chines to equip at least 15 per cent. of
the New York polling places this year,
but, following the disagreement of the
Board of Elections, came the refusal
of the Automatic Registering Machine
Corporation, of Jamestown, N. Y., to
sell ‘machines to a city ‘‘ where there

is every prospect of obstruction and liti-
gation staring it in it's face.”

John R. Voorhis, President of the
of Elections, who has opposed
making a contract with the Jamestown
firm manufacturing voting machines,
declared last night that he was not sur-
prised that the firm had refused” to con-
tinue its efforts to get its machine in-
stalled in this city. He said he had
opposed this particular inachine because
he believed it was too costly.

if the machine was forced upon the
city, Mr. Voorhis said, litigation would
be sure to follow, as the financial offi-
clals would not agree to the price. Op-
portunity, he said, should be given to
manufacturers to submit other types of
machines, as he understood they could

must be accompanied by an opinion in
writing to the Attorney General, set-
ting forth the reasons for the proposed
action. This means that cnly the most
carefully considered judgments of the
advisory council, embodied in written |
statements, will determine the course of
the Department of Justice in dealing
with all miscellaneous cases.

“Written decisions and opinions as to
the proposed initiation or disposal of
cases are also required to be made by
the Board of Administration and Re-
view. To this board the Attorney Gen-

be manufactured at a much lower cost.
A delay of a year in the installation of
voting machines might be a good thing,
he added, as a better type of machine
might be evolved.

The Commissioner denied that politics
had influenced his attitude in any way.
Only one political party, he said, had
favored the type of machine in question,
The Democrats, he said, had never taken
a Stand in the matter, except those
Democratic members of the Election

Board who had opposed it on account
of its price.

For years the largest circulation among Chicago
newspapers (city and suburban as well as total)
has been that of The Sunday Tribune. For years
the largest week-day circulation (exclusive of
Sunday) has been that of The Daily Tribune.

During May and June, 1922, The Tribune has
won another “FIRST” in that its net paid city
and suburban circulation on week days (exclu-
sive of Sunday) exceeded that of the next paper.

Tribune Supreme in
Advertising Lineage

During the first six months of 1922 The Chicago
Tribune printed more than 35% of all the ad-
vertising carried by the six Chicago newspapers.

During the first six months of 1922 The Tribune
has gained 4,235 columns over the correspond-
ing period of 1921, but the second Chicago
paper has Jost 767 columns.

In local display advertising The Tribune gained
2,215 columns over 1921, but the second paper
lost 1,170 columns.

In want advertising The Tribune gained 952
columns over 1921, but the second paper lost
395 columns.

From President Harding.

THE WHITE HOUSE,
Washington, D. C., July .20.
Hoyt ‘Miller, ‘care Tue New York
“Times, New York:
“News of your distinguished father’s

~ @eath.. brings me a sense of personal

loss, because of long-maintained ad-
miration-for his public services and
Professional abilities. His was a career
ofthe type which, journalists. and pub-
licists might well emulate ~-by efforts
at that. reasonableness, modern con-
structive: effort and. unfailing courage
which he displayed. I tender sincerest
condolences in your loss.
WARREN G. HARDING.

‘From. Governor Miller.

Albany, N. Y., July 20.
The country has lost one of its great
men and journalism one of its soundest |
Philosophical. thinkers. Mr. Miller was
ene of our ablest exponents of constitu-
tional government. .I ‘deeply sympathize
with you in your loss,
NATHAN L, MILLER, Governor.

I learn with profound sorrow of Mr.

JAMES' M. COX.

From Ex-Senator Depew.

Geepest sympathy. The world loses much

CHAUNCEY M. DEPEW.

From Will H. Hays.

Chicago, July 20.
Just learned of Mr. Miller’s death and
want to send just this word of apprecia-
tion: Charles. R. Miller was a great
man, a-great editor and a distinguished
citizen; as. such we mourn for him.
Personally I really feel his loss most
keenly. He was uniformly so kind to
me, and many times in the last few
years when I have talked deeply to him
on matters in which I was interested,
he has always had a sympathetic and
kind understanding that has meant very
much to me. Most deeply, indeed, do I
feel his loss personally.
WILL H. HAYS,

From The Day

Two days ago died in New York one
of the anonymous powers. of modern
democracy—tne editor of a _ powerful
newspaper. Charles Ransom Miller, as
director of the policy of THE NEw YorK
Times, and himsélf one of its most ca-
pable exponents, was little heard of ex-
cept in professional circles which are
acquainted with the inside of news-
paperdom. Yet day in, day out, for
something like forty years, he gave the
mot d’ordre to an-organ which today
is admittedly one of the most influential
in the world.

As the editor of THr New YORK
Times Mr. Miller was a powerful con-
servative influence. Apart from the in-
dividual question which THr TIMES
helped with its influence to decide, it
has so steadily maintained an attitude
of political and social conservatism as
to have become the mouthpiece of the
American standpatter. In that respeet
THe New YORK Times occupies a unique
position. Both by virtue of its mag-
nificent. news service and by the se-
riousness of its tone, it has climbed to
that position—comparable to that held
by The Times of England and by Le
Temps of France. * * *

In the creation of that force,
its direction, Charles Ransom
was an important factor.

From The Jewish Daily News.

Charles Ransom °~Miller belonged to
what has been termed the old school
of journalism. He was the statesman in
daily newspaperdom. Scholarly, imbued
with a. high sense of responsibility, a
thinker, wielding a trenchant pen, he
helped to make history by interpreting
the trend of thought and of current
events to his readers.

Naturally a conservative, schooled in
the classics, Charles Ransom Miller
brought to bear upon the editorial con-
duct of THE New YorRK TIMES a view-
point which, while not always accept-
able, was premised upon deep thought
and -an earnest sincerity. He was the
very opposite of the sensational shallow
journalist who seeks temporary glory in
the shrick and the stirring up of ani-
mosities.

Charles Ransom Miller was a national
figure, and it may be said without ex-
aggeration that he was of international
importance. He wrote under the cloak
of anonymity. This was in harmony
with the school of journalism of which
he was so fine an exponent. This did not
imply fear“or lack of courage but rather
was the result of the thought that the
great daily newspaper represents not
merely a personal opinion, but a com-
ination of opinidns resulting from study,
understanding and a keen desire to
further human progress.

From The Buffalo News.

It is a commonplace to newspaper
men, but apparently a recurring source
of mild wonderment to the public that
the great men of the newspaper world
are unknown, except to the guild.

Charles Ransom Miller was one of the
truly great men in America. Yet it is
probable that not one in a hundred of
the readers of THe New Yorx Times
know even his name. Easy fame lay
within his grasp. Men with a tithe of
his ability are known from coast to
coast. _He preferred to remain true to
the editorial tradition of impersonality.

Speaking with the impressive author-
ity of THE New Yorx Times, the pres-
tige of which he did as much as any
man to build, his influence spread over
the course of four decades is beyond
all,computation. Charles Ransom Miller
was one of. the figures who make us
proud to say ‘‘ We, too, are newspaper
men.”’

From the |Philadelphia Evening Ledger.

The summary. of the attainments of
the late Charles R. Miller, for more n
forty years editor of THz NEW YoRK
TIMES, ‘may surprise those outside of
newspaper offices by its revelation of
the extent of the mental] equipment re-
garded as necessary to qualify a man
to direct the policy of a great journal.

Mr. Miller was a Doctor of Laws.’ The
degree was conferred on him by Dart-
mouth College seventeen years ago, in
recognition of his learning. He was
first a fine classical scholar. He spoke
and read French, German, Italian, Span-
ish and Russian, He had a mastery of
the political history of his own and
other countries. He was an expert on
international law and on’ foreign re-
lations. His knowledge of cconomics
and of literature was as broad as that
of many. college professors. There were
a score of subjects on’ which he could
have lectured to college classes more il-
luminatingly than the men hired to
do it.

He had equipped himself this way be-
cause it was-his business to know ‘the
subjects which his newspaper had to
discuss, Just as the editors and editorial
writers of other newspapers have
equipped themselves by constant study
{in order to discuss intelligently the
questions which are continually arising.
These editors are as well groundéd in
their subjects as any ore, and they are
in closer touch with the changing cur-
rents’ of opinion than any other group
of men.

It has been fashionable to regret the
disappearance of Greeleys and the Ray-
monds from journalism, but Mr. Miller
would have held his own with these men
in their specialties and he could have
written all around them lot of
other subjects.

ism. Ever mindful of the fact that

Defender of Central Park.

To the Editor of The New York Times:

Charles R. Miller was, perhaps, the
best and most powerful friend Central
Park has had during a third of a cen-
tury. This I feel should -be said at
this ‘time and said emphatically ‘by
some one who has known the facts
through all these years. This should
never be forgotten by: the lovers of
Central Park.

He, of all men, knew the real mean-
ing of Central Park. How much it
meant for the children and mothers on
the east side as well as the lovers of
country sights and sounds was always
in his mind. Fully realizing as few
have ever done the profound, true and |
abiding art of Olmsted and -Vaux, the |
designers of Central Park, Charles R.
Miller had an open mind for all changes
necessary to meet new conditions. Al-
ways and ever, though, he recognized
the fine artistic instinct that inspired
the designers when they sought to bring
country life to the city. It wa8S a great
boon for the New York press to have
a champion of Central Park in such a
dominant position as that held by him.
He defended the Park a hundred, nay,
a thousand times, with such high zeal
and ideals and sueh a forceful, con-
vincing and able style that there was
in all the country no such power -ex-
ercised in such a masterly fashion for
the purpose in view and through such
a long period of years.

I know. Charles -R.- Miller loved Cen-
tral Park and was able to.do wonders
to save it time and time again. Few
have been in such a good position to
judge of his value as I have been and
I want to testify to what I know and
feel at this time of his passing. —

Yours very truly,
SAMUEL PARSONS,

GOMPERS SEES. REBUKE
TO GLD GUARD POLICY

Declares Nebraska Primary Again
Shows the People Won't Stand
for Repression.

Special to The New York Times.
WASHINGTON, July 20.—Samuel Gom-
pers, President of the American Federa-
tion of Labor, sees the primary election

results in Nebraska as a fresh rebuke
to Old Guard tactics, ‘‘ which might be
borne in mind while the Government tis
embarking upon a. course of repression

by force and upon a course of military }-

dictatorship.”’

‘* Political opinion,’’ said Mr. Gompers,
‘“‘is being registered against the kind of
Governmental policy now being mani-
fested in the coal and railroad. strikes.
This opinion is expressing itself as rap-
idly as opportunity offers,

“The Old Guard, as it is called, has
just been beaten in Nebraska. Congress-
man Albert W. Jefferis, who was defeat-
ed for the nomination for United States
Senator in that State, was possessed of
a good legislative record, but ne weht
into the campaign arm in arm with the

Olicies of the President which are be-

ng.so may displayed in the great in-
dustrial crisis.‘ The people, including
the workers. of Nebraska, voted down
those policies.

‘The primaries have not failed thus
far to show the revulsion of the peo-
ple against. Old Guard tactics. This
might with profit be borne in mind
while the Government is embarking
upon a course of repression by force
and upon a course of military dictator-
ship for the purpose of beating down
workers who have a just and burning
grievance,”’

Press).—Political observers watching the
count of the vote in Tuesday’s primary
in the race for the Republican Guberna-

torial nomination between Adam McMul-
len of Beatrice and Charles I, Randall of
Randolph ex es the opinion tonight
that it would take the official count,
with mail votes permitted under the
Absent Voters’ law, to decide the out-
come, so harrow was the margin sepa-
rating the contestants.

committeeman, progressive Republican,
was strengthening the plurality by which
he won the Republican United States
Senatorial nomination tioin Representa-
tive Albert W. Jefferis, regarded as>a
conservative Republican. Jefferis ran
13,000 behind Howell in 1,740 precincts,
and was only 600 votes ahead of Clar-
ence A. Davis, Attorney General, also a
progressive Republican, with C. H. Gus-
tafson, head of the United States Grain
aromers: ‘Inc., trailing.7,000 votes behind.

ONE PENALTY FOR STRIKING.

It is stated that the railway shop-
men were willing to’ call off their
strike and go back to work provided
their ‘‘ seniority ’’ rights were _Te-
stored to them. But the railroad ex-
ecutives refused to assent to this con-
dition. It might seem a trifling mat-
ter, but it is not. Many new men
bave been employed, and under the
terms of their engagement are entitled
to the privileges of seniority, compris-
ing the right to be assigned first to
repair work that comes into the shops.
Moreover, the strikers had been duly
and definitely warned that if they left
the employ of the roads they would
lose their seniority rights, and could
return to work only as if they were
new employés.

Evidently a principle is involved, im-
portant not only to the public but to
the unions. Too many strikes are en-
tered upon light-heartedly, the men
being ready to ‘‘ take a chance ”’ in
the belief that, even if the strike be
lost, they can have \their jobs again
as if nothing had happened. That, in
fact, has often. occurred, especially
during the recent years when there
was a shortage of labor. Conditions
are now different, and it may be a
wholesame thing to drive home the
lesson’ that there are, after all, cer-
tain penalties for a reckless strike.

lives. The fact that the Council of

support of the majority of the popu-

COUNTRY AND CITY.

The statement of the Census Bu-
reau that only 29.9 per cent. of the
people of the United States live on
farms may disturb those who think
that the trend from the. land thus
indicated is portentous. But whatever
the migration to the city means in its
moral and economic consequences, the

|fact that the number of persons en-

gaged in agricultural pursuits has
decreased in the last hundred years
from 87 per. cent. to 30 per cent. is
not in. itself ominous. The decline is
due in part to an increase in the agri-
cultural productivity of the average
farmer.

In the early days an entire family on
the farm produced little if any more
than enough for its own subsistence.
Now one family produces sufficient

|for three families, and perhaps even

more. The other two, or three, are
free to get fuel for all; to manufac-
ture, transport, buy and sell; to care
for the sick as doctors or nurses; to
see that justice is done among all;
to furnish information, to teach, to
preach, to study, to carry on scientific
research, to bring art in all its forms
to the enrichment and adornment of
life. So the actual number engaged
in agriculture, up to the point of
maximum productivity, is roughly in
inverse ratio to the degree of its de-
velopment. And this development in
turn connotes in a general way the

sort of civilization that rests upon it. |

In China 70 per cent. or more of the
people are engaged in farming, and yet
there are not enough farmers to till
all the available land, so crude are
their methods of production. With us
30 per cent. release 70 per cent. for
other employment; thirty millions re-
lease seventy millions.

The thing of prime consequence is
that those thirty millions shall have a
fair share of the fruits of the civiliza-
tion that has its roots in the soil of
the farm. The provision and main-
tenance of better rural schools is
essential. It is of national importance
that the public now give more serious
attention to such rural school pro-
grams as are prepared for New York
and Pennsylvania. This better farm,
better farm home, better rural school
movement is widespread and is even
further on its way in the States of the
Middle West. As indication of this
new spirit among the farmers them-
selves, it is reported that a meeting
was held a fortnight ago out in
Illinois, at which 20,000 or 25,000
were gathered to celebrate and further
the work of the farm and home bu-
reaus. Better farmers may indeed
mean fewer farmers. And a trend
from the farm may be a sign of a
higher state of farm development—a
trend which is good or bad, according
to what happens at the city end.
