The Drama

In intention at
least, nothing could
Ancient be more admirable
than the stand taken

and Modern. by Swarthmore Col-
lege with regard to the dress of its wo-
men students. ‘‘ Extremes or eccentric-
ities in style of the dress and of the
coiffure,”’ writes the Dean to mothers of
ithe coming class, “ are not indicative of
the good taste which college women
should preserve.”’

But what shall one say looking Dack-
ward upon the habits of other years? It
is not necessary to invoxe stomacher
and crinoline. Time was when young
ladies at Swarthmore and elsewhere
wore sleeves that flanked their shoulders
as if with two gross hams. A little iater
they wore hats that perched forward
over a fuzzy bang like a pancake crest-
ing an ocean breaker. Albums of old
snapshots ate mere chambers of such
horrors. Yet the wearers were still
young ladies—the very same, in fact,
who now write that Swarthmore, or
Wellesley, or Smith, “has a tradition
which must be maintained in the future
as it has been in the past.”

The real complaint against votartes of
short skirts and bobbed hair, one sus-
pects, is that they have ventured to
have an eccentricity of dress or of coif-
fure that differs from the eccentricities
of their elders. At Vassar lately, when
a trainload of old grads alighted, a
young thing on the platform was heard
|}to whisper, ‘Here come the alumnae,
| with their corsets and their ears! ”’

The head of the Society
for the Suppression of
Vice, having had Mr.
THOMAS SELTZER arrested
for publishing the works
of ScHNITZLER and D. H. LAWRENCE, has
now gone on to prosecute another firm
for selling the Satyricon of PEeTRoNIuS.
The publishers say that the book is not
| sold to the general public; what criterion
they use in the selection of permitted
purchasers is not stated.

Such a prosecution ought to cause re-
consideration of the principles of our
laws against obscene publications. In
any ordinary definition of that word
PETRONIUs is certainly obscene; and yet
he is read by many who are merely an-
noyed by his obscenities. The extant
fragments of what must have been a
long book reveal a brildant talent; they
contain excellent writing, some admira-
ble literary and artistic criticism; above
all, they afford evidence such as can be
found nowhere else as to the social
conditions in certain classes of society
at Rome in the first century A. D. It
would be a serious loss to human knowl-
edge to suppress PErrroNIus, whatever
may be thought of SCHNITZLER and D. H.
LAWRENCE,

It used to be assumed by courts which
construed the law that persons who
could read the classical languages were
already corrupt beyond hope of redemp-
tion; hence the obscene classics were
usually allowed to circulate without in-
terference. Mr. SUMNER has now at-
tacked that interpretation of the law.
And he is quite right, if one assumes—
as he must—that in a work containing
obscene passages nothing else is read,
and that matter which might pervert
some readers must be withheld from all

readers.

May Be Found in “ Records of the
War of the Rebellion.”
To the Editor of The New York Times:

There has been a good deal of misin-
formation published in the papers of the
country recently about the endorsement
by the Confederate reunion of a book
that contained matter supposed to be
unjust to Mr. Lincoln, As I am in pos-
session of the facts in the case, also of
a few of these books, I will be glad to
straighten this matter out for y of
your readers desiring to learn the truth.

In the first place, this book is not a
history, nor was it written by Colonel
Huger W. Jackson of Curryville, Va., as
thé writers of the letters‘in the papers
seem to think, but it is a small pamphlet
written by a Confederate naval officer,
Captain H. W. Johnstone of Idyl-
wild, Ga.

The data in this. little book did not
originate. with Captain Johnstone; he
simply culled them from the ‘“‘Records of
the War of the Rebellion’’ and put them
in convenient shape for the reader. This
many-volumed record, as you doubtless
knew, was published by the United
States Government and supposed for
that reason to be authentic. Any one
willing to take the time to fefret out
this matter can get this same informa-
tion by reading the ‘Records of the
War of the Rebellion.”

The data in this little pamphlet are all
based on Lincoln’s signed telegrams as
reported in this Government record, and
it. goes without saying that if the in-
ferences drawn from these telegrams are
uncomplimentary to Mr. Lincoln, then
the responsibility for this offense harks
back to the United States Government,
which published these telegrams, and
has put this book in néarly every library
in the country.

There are doubtless many libraries in
your city that possess copies of this
Government record, so it will be easy
for any one who desires ta do so to
verify this matter for himself.

The “leader” that appeared in your
paper on this subject was, in my judg-
ment, more discriminating than that in
any other paper that has come under
my notice. M. D. CARTER.
| -Uppefville, Va., July 13, 1922.

Dickman Heads Body Named to,

Drop 1,700 Army Officers.

WASHINGTON, July 20.—The Board
of General Officers’ to supervise reduc-
tion of the number of regular officers
of the army to the figures prescribed
by: Congress will be headed by Major
Gen. Joseph T. Dickman, retired, as
President.s Other members of the board
will be Major Gen. Merritt W. Ireland,
Surgeon General; Major Gen. Henry P.
‘McCain, retired, former Adjutant Gen-
éral, and, Brig. Gens. Andre W. Brew-
ster and Ernest Hinds.

‘The magnitude and importance of
the work of this board have caused the
utmost care to be observed in the selec-
tion of its members,’”’ the War Départ-
ment’s announcement said. It added
that the department had sought to pro-
vide for ‘‘a thoroughly just and im-
partial ’’ survey by the board and in the
make-up of the board had excluded of-
ficers now or recently *‘ closely identi-
fied with the present War Department
administration,’’ and included officers
not graduates of West Point and an of-
ficer who did not serve abroad during
the war. The board also represents the
major branches of the army in that men
who have served in the infantry, the ar-
tillery, the cavalry and in the staff de-
partments are members.

It will be the function of the board to
pass upon the records of all officers in
the army, with the exception of Second
Lieutenants, and determine the relative
value of such officers to. the Govern-
ment. Those for any reason of least
value, in the judgment of the board, will
be separated from the.active service by
Dec. 15 next. They will be retired for
physical disability, reduced one step in
rank or honorably discharged .with a
yee # pay in lieu of retirement ben-
efits.

It is ‘estimated that probably more
than 1,700 officers now on the rolls of
the regular army and ineluding officers

RETAIL FOOD COST RISES.

Average Increase of 1 Per Cent.
From May 15 to June 15.

WASHINGTON, July 20.—The retail
eost of food to the average family in
the United States Increased 1 per cent.
from May.15 to June 15, according to a
report today by the Bureau of Labor
Statistics of the Department of Labor.

Qf forty-three food articles computed
in the average, increases,in twenty-one
ranged from 20 per cent\ for potatoes
to one-half of 1 per cent. for bananas.
Decreases in twelve ranged from 18 per
cent. for onions to 1 per cent. for canned
peas, while prices for the others re-
mained practically stationary.

The largest increase in food prices for
the month was 4 per cent. for Detroit.
Of the ten cities out of fifty-one show-
ing a decrease in the average price,
none exceeded i per cent.

SEAPLANES QUICKLY LANDED

New Naval Device Stops Them on
the Decks of Warships.

WASHINGTON, July 20.—Perfection
of a device to enable en airplane going
60 miles an hour, to land om the deck of
a ship, was announced today by the
Navy Department. For the iast few
months the naval air service has been
experimenting secretly at Hampton
Roads with the device on a dummy
ship’s deck.

The device, which it is said will per-
mit the safe landing of any type of air-
Mahe equipped with landing gear in uSe
on a number of
wires placed across the ship’s deck,
weights being attached to the — ends.
Hooks descending from the bottom of
the airplanc, engage the wires. The in-
creasing weight exerts a brake effect on
the speed of the plane.

In one of the experiments a small air-
— was. brought to a stop within 38
eet.

The Minnesota Afloat.
To the Editor of The New. York Times:

In your Book Raevipw AND M4GazInge of the
16th, in the article entitled ‘* Under-Sea
Men,’’ the author states that the battleship
Minnesota was sunk. This is an error.

While sweeping German mines off the Jer-
sey coast with the U. S. minesweeper King-
fisher the U. S. minesweeper Teal received
wireless orders to go to the assistance of
the steamship Minnesota off Fenwick Island
Lightship.

The Teal proceeded as directed, and when
we sighted the battleship Minnesota she was
listed to starboard, but was proceeding un-
der her own steam. She reached the League
Island Navy Yard at Philadelphia,

Shortly after the Teal was ordered to the
same yard for repairs. This gave me an
opportunity to visit the Minnesota in dry
dock, and there was a hole in her starboard
bow ‘‘big enough to drive a horse’ and
wagon through.”

ROBERT B. PETERS,
Ex-Chief Gunner’s Mate U. 8. 8. Teal, Mine-
sweeper No. 23.
Brooklyn, July 17, 1922.

An Elemental Explosive.
To the Editor of The New York Times:

I read in this morning’s Times ‘‘ that the
explosion of a case of magnesium powder
is believed to be the cause of the Jane
Street fire.”

Now, magnesium may be an ingredient of
explosive mixtures, but it is not explosive
by itself. An element cannot, in the chem-
ical sense, be explosive per se. The only

exception is liquid ozone. C. PARODI.
New York, July 19, 1922.

RESTORATION.

When friends betray, and love grows
sour,
When men and women fail,
Peace comes within the hermit’s bower;
The world of books I hail.

And when the printed page turns cold,
When soul’ departs from words,
My comrades rise in field and fold,

"Mid animals and birds.

But when dark memory my spirit tries,
And opens wide my scars,
I lift mine eyes beyond the skies,
In union with the stars.
LOUIS Il. NEWMAN,

Administration Stands Firmly
by Its Demand for Guarantees
Before Recognition Is Given.

LAND SEIZURE GOES ON

Present Situation One in Which
Friction Between the Two Coun-
tries Might Easily Arise.

Special te The New York Times.

WASHINGTON, July 20.—A high
spokesman of the Administration today
furnished an informal summary of the
situation {nvolving the issues between
this country and Mexico, from which it
is apparent that recognition of Mexico
by the American Government is as far
off as ever unless the Obregon Govern-
ment translates informal assurances
into action and gives those definite and
precise guarantees of security which are
insisted upon rigidly by the American
Government,

The statement of the case today was
the more significant, becausé it came en
the heels of the recent visit to the White
House and State Department of Adolfo
de la Huerta, Mexican Minister of Fi-
nance, to whom the attitude of the
Washington Government was again
clearly explained during his conference
of nearly two hours with Secretary of
State Hughes. The hope is expressed

here that upon his return tg Mexico
City Sefior de la Huerta -make a
report to President Obregon: that would
be followed by affirmative action by the
Mexican Government of such character
as to warrant recognition.

The American Government’s position

is that recognition depends on the Mex-~

icans. If they ‘wish prompt reco: on
they can give prompt guarantees, The
longer they delay the action for which
Secretary Hughes, as spokesman for
President Harding, is waiting the longer
recognition will be delayed.

Not less than five distinct. opportuni-—
ties have been afforded the Obregon -

Government to demonstrate in a prac-
tical way its desire to resume diplomatic

relations with the United States, it was.

stated. The first of these was the pro-
posal made by Secretary of State Hughes
that the two nations conclude a trea
of amity and commerce. Though s
suggestion was made more than a year
and a half ago it has not been acce

by the Mexican Government; the
pointed out. Throughout tne time which
has elapsed since the proposal was
made, this Government has maintained
a discreet silence, it was stated, in
order that Obregon might be free to
work out his affairs in his own way,
without embarrassment fiom this end.
Nevertheless, the problem apparently is
no nearer solution than
ations were undertaken.

Debt Agreement Not Complete.

The second big opportunity afforded
the Obregon Government, the official
said, was in connection with the recent
international banking agreement con-
cluded at New York between Finance

Minister de la Huerta and representa-
tives of the international ereditors of
Mexico. ‘Tnis agreement, which was
heralded as a step in the direction of
recognition, has not been approved by
Obregon, who apparently is unable, or
unwilling, to act in the face of a re-
luctant Congress.

The third case mentioned had to do
with the agreement entered into by
American oil men at Mexico City with
the Mexican authorities.

The fotirth case was the decisions by
the Mexitan Supreme Court be
upon the question of the retroactivity of
Article 27 o¥ the Mexican Constitution.
Numerous statements have been made,
it was pointed-out, to. the effect that
these decisions afforded the guarantees
against confiscation which the American
Government has been seeking. Never-
theless, the official continued, it has
proved impossible, despite weeks of de-
lay, for this Government to obtain
copies of tne text of these decisions or
to find out in a specific and definite way
exactly how comprehensive they are in
scope,

Action on agrarian lands was the fifth
point discussed by the officlal. Ex-
propriation, which is regarded here as
not being in accordance with American
principles, apparently is sanctioned by
the laws and constitutions of some of
the Mexican States, it was stated, and
the Obregon Government either is unable
or umwiilling to prevent the carrying
out of these laws.

President Obregon, in speeches and in
interviews, has many times asserted
that Article 27 will not be applied retro-
actively. Such assertions were welcome
to this Government, but inasmuch as
they were personal and informal, were
not regarded as sufficient.

The United States proposed, therefore,
a treaty of amity and commerce which
would definitely safeguard American
rights. This treaty, President Ob im
stated, he had no authority to sign. 6
fact that he said he had no authority to
do this greatly detracted, in the opin-
ion of the American Government, from
the previous statements of the Mexican
President that no retroactive effect
would be given to the Constitutional pro-
visions.

Since negotiations began with the
Mexican Government, there have been
numerous instances of confiscation of
American agrarian holdings in Mexico,
it was officiahy admitted today. The
term used by the Mexican Government,
it was explained, is expropriation, but
expropriation implies payment, and no
just payment has been made in numer-
ous cases, and the proceeding, therefore,
becomes confiscation. In many instances
valuation was based on taxes which re-
sulted in only a nominal value being
placed on the land, and payment at the
merely nominal figure was then offered
in practically worthless bonds.

This Government has no objection to
expropriation in the interests of some
worthy public policy, as for example,

| providing the peons with lands, but {t

| tion be made when the validly acquired

| Company, which notified the Transit

ltated by Wall Street or by the oil in-
\terests, but is determined by American
lrights of whatever nature they may be.

Persons are going about the ¢ 4
the Administration spokesman 4
today, talking about things which should
be done by Mexico. as if they had al-
ready been done. This Government does
not wish to be put in the poetics of
appearing to dictate to Mexico, but at
the same time it_is unwilling that the
Mexican people should get the idea that
we can be fooled into believing certain
essential conditions have been met when
they have not.

When loose conversation is indulged
in as to, agreements havi been made
on the Mexican external debt, or agree-

must be remembered that the agreement
is not complete until-Obregon or the

-* OF ‘CONEY’ IN PARK

Stewart Browne, in Letter to
Hylan, Says Hearings Have
Become “Public Scoldings.”’

OPPOSES $600,000 VOTED

Charges Estimate Board Put Citl-
zens to Vexatious Delays—Lew-
isohn Protests Building in Park.

The Board of Estimate’s action on the
Proposed Central Park war meniorial,
for which $600,000 was appropriated
Wednesday, despite the protests of civic
associations and individuals interested
in the parks, was attacked yesterday
by Stewart Browne of the United
Real Estate, Owners’ Association. Mr.
Browne, in a letter ‘to Mayor Hylan,
declared that hearings of the board had
degenerated into ‘‘ public scoldings.’’

Mr. Browne was one of those present
at Wednesday’s hearing. He quit the
meeting after the Mayor had threatened
to have him seated by force.

The Parks and Playgrounds Associa-
tion, it was said yesterday, would have
a statement to make with regard to the
Board of Estimate’s action. George
Gordon Battle, President of the asso-
ciation,.is in Maine. William Brad-
ford Roulstone, Chairman of the Parks
Committee, represented the association
at the board meeting.

Mr..Browne’s letter follows:

UNITED REAL ESTATE OWNERS’
ASSOCIATION,
280 Broadway,
New York City, July 20, 1922.
Hon. John F. Hylan, Mayor of the
City of New York:
My Dear Mayor Hylan: While John
F. Hylan in private life and Mayor
Hylan in individual interviews are ex-
tremely courteous, considerate and
pleasing personalities, the Mayor of
the city at which are euphoniously
miscalied public hearings of the
Board of Estimate is extremely dis-
courteous and inconsiderate and makes
a ‘bully’ Chairman.
For instance: The people of the city
are intensely interested in the pro-
osed combination war memorial and
ittle Coney Island in Central Park
and the Art and Music Temple on Sev-
enth, Avenue, between Fifty-sixth and
Fifty-ninth Streets, and which have
been on the calendar for public hear-
ings for three separate Board of Bsti-
mate meetings. Fully 1,000 people ap-
peared at the first to be politely told
for the first time that the meeting
Was postponed until the next week,
when public notice could have been
given the day before. The next week
arrived and, owing to the sad and un-
expected death of Borotigh President
Cahill, the meeting was very properly
postponed, but the audience was kept
waiting fully an hour before such an-
nouncement was made.
At yesterday's hearing were at least
ten of the principal civic and realty
organizations present, as you and your
colleagues well know, to. protest
against the above two proposais.
Your meéeting continued from 10:30
A. M. to 5 P. M., and although your
board had predetermined to give no
public hearing on these two matters,
you kept the representatives of these
ten organizations kicking their heels
and wasting their time, to be discour-
teously told by you at 5 P. M. that
there would be no public hearings on
these two matters except public hear-
ings to hear and not to be heard, and
you jammed them through in spite of
protests. In doing this you were ex-
tremely inconsiderate in not making
such announcement at the beginning
of the meeting—10:30 A. M.—and your
only apparent reason was that you
thought you could tire the opponents
out by such dilatory tactics.
Permit me courteously to suggest
that your public hearings are worse
than you designate them, viz.: Pub-
lic hearings to hear and not to be
heard, or ‘‘ public listenings,’” but in |
addition they have degenerated into
‘“‘public scoldings’’ and appeals to
class prejudice.
You said that yesterday’s votes
didn’t commit the board to anything.
They door do not according to your
desire. =e can rescind, modify or
let them stand. Don’t you think it is
absurd to vote $600,000 for something
or other that you say you don’t know
anything about? But you can’t fool
me with that statement. The Jamaica
Bay Boulevard was to be paid for by
Queens, but before the last election
it was by your 'board’s resolution
made a city-wide charge. There are
hundreds of similar cases. Faithfully
yours,
STEWART BROWNE, President.

RUTH JONES HEARD.

Young Violinist Makes Her Prelimi-
nary Debut in Chicago.

Special to The New York Times.

CHICAGO, July 20.—Ruth Jones, a
violinist, who is said to be planning an
entrance-upon the professional concert
stage next season, made her preliminary
début at the Ziegfeld Theatre this morn-
ing. Miss Jones is the wife of Richard
G. Knott, editor of The Louisville Bve-
ning Post, and is a pupil of Leopold
Auer. Apparently, she will go on well
equipped. She has acquired all the

requisites of full bodied tone and. a
technique that makes light of the diffi-
culties in her path, and she has in addi-
tion a breezy, vigorous manner of plan-
ning that is personal. :

Her program would seem to have
been chosen with those characteristics
fn mind. It included the Vitali Cha-
conne, the Lalo ‘‘Symphonie Espa-
gnole,’’ which can be successful only
when the player approaches it in the
attitude of treating it as a lively game,
and a pair of groups of shorter pieces,
some interesting, others harmless but no
doubt necessary. Because of her own
energetic individuality, Miss Jones gives
more promise of definite accomplish-
ments in her artistic career than the
e@verage, and this with many other good
young violinists in’ mind.

Countess of Cassillis Says Duke of

Roy, had died childless in Wakefield
Lodge, Stony Startford, England, on
May 10, 1912. He was the eldest of
four brothers, one of whom, Alfred
William Maitland Fitz Roy, because the
eighth Duke of Grafton upon the death

FARRAR ASKS 99600
FROM LOU TRLLEGEN

Opera Singer Suing for Divorce
Says Husband Failed to
Repay Loans.

ANSWER DENIES DEBTS

Denial of Plea for Details of Reply
Reveals Action Filed Several
Months Ago.

Geraldine Farrar, opera singer, who is
suing her husband, Lou Tellegen, actor,

for divorce, filed a new suit against him
in the Supreme Court several months
ago, in which she demands the repay-
ment of $9,600 alleged to have been lent
to Tellegen during the. four years they
lived together.

This did not become known until yes-
terday, when an application by Miss
Farrar to coinpel her husband to give
particulars of the defense in his answer
mailed to her attorneys last month was
denied by Justice Donnelly. The papers
also show that Max D. Steuer is now
acting as attorney for Tellegen. The
answer claimed ail the money was re-
paid.

In her petition asking for particulars,
the opera singer demanded that her hus-
band tell when, where, by whom, to
whom, and in what manner the pay-
ments were made, because the only in-
formation given in his answer is a gen-
eral allegation that ‘‘each and every
sum of money that the defendant bor-
rowed from the plaintiff he duly paid to
the plaintiff, and there is no Indebted-
ness existing from the defendant to the
plaintiff.”

The petition stated that Miss Farrar
is suing for the following loans: $2,000 on
$1,000, July 1, 1921. The date of the last
alleged loan was shortly before Miss
Farrar is said to have ousted her hus-
band from her residence in this city,
which resulted in his filing a separation
suit in August and her divorce action in
New York County. The two actions were
joined later and will be tried here to-
gether.

Mr. Steuer, for Tellegen, in opposing
the application, pointed out decisions by
the Appellate Division stating that the
caurt will not require a defendant to
give particulars of defenses of payment
‘unless very special reasons appear.”’

SIR HARRY LAUDER COMING.

He May Be’ Accompanied by Sir
Thomas Lipton, Wm. Morris Says.

William Morris, theatrical manager,
who returned on the Homeric of the
White Star Line yesterday -vith Mrs.
Morris and William Morris Jr., an-
nounced that Sir Harry Lauder would
be in New York early in September, his
next American tour. Sir Thomas Lip-
ton expected to accompany Sir Harry
across and issue a challenge for an-
other international yacht race, Mr. Mor-
ris said. The comedian and the yachts-
man at present were on a fishing trip
on the east coast of England. 7

After making a twenty-two weeks tour
of this country, Sir Harry would go to
Australia, and later to South Africa,
Mr. Morris said. He told of the gift of
‘““the crookedest cane in the world”
from the Prince of Wales to Lauder.

‘‘The Prince brought back the cane
from Japan, where it -was presented to
him by a group of Japanese noblemen,”’
Mr. Morris said. ‘‘ Knowing Sir Harry‘s
penchant for weird canes, the Prince
sent it to him on his return from the
world tour. In return Sir Harry sent
the Prince of Wales a handsome stick.”

Mr. Morris said he had secured the
rights of a Hindu drama by Narengien
Pal, a son of a native ruler. He said
the play would be produced here next
season with a troupe of Hindu actors.
The drama dealt with the problems of
India and offered a solution, Mr. Mor-
ris said.

Daniel Frohman Gives a Birthday
Party for Stage Veteran.

Daniel Frohman gave a birthday par-
ty atop of the Lyceum Theatre last
evening for the veteran actor, F. F.
Mackay, who is 90 years old and still
active as Executive Chairman of the
Actors’ Fund. The guests invited in-
cluded Sam Scribner, Milton Nobles,
Ralph Delmore, Major A. B. Reinold,
Charles B. Wells, Walter Vincent and
W. Cc. Austin.

David Belasco, rehearsing a play be-
low stairs, went up to. offer congratu-
lations to Mr. Mackay, who was stage
manager of the old California Theatre
when young Belasco was the assistant
in their early days out West.

" Orlando S. Isbell.

Orlando S. Isbell, Vice President and
Secretary of the Lawyers’ Mortgage
Company, died Wednesday evening in a
private sanitarium at 393 Central Park
West.after a month’s illness. Born 56
years ago in New Haven, Conn., he
graduated from Yale in 1873, prepared
for the bar at Yale, and began practice
in Denver, Col. In 1901 he moved to
this city and became associated with
the Lawyers’ Mortgage Company. He
was unmarried and lived with his
mother and a married sister at 250 West
Ninety-third Street.

Miss Belle H. Bennett.

RICHMOND, Ky., July 20.—Miss Belle
H. Bennett, for many years prominent
in the work of the Methodist Episcopal
Church in the United States, died here
this morning after a lingering illness.
She was the founder of the Scarrett
Bible and Training School in Kansas
City, Mo., and was a leader in estab-
lishing schools for mountaineers and in-
digent girls;. also city missions, known
as Wesley Houses, in many industrial
centres of the South.
dent of the Women's Missionary Council
of the M. FE. Church and had been Presi-
dent of the Woman's Board of Home
Missions.

Edward H. Blake.

BANGOR, Me., July 20.—Edward H.
Blake, President of the Merchants’ Na-
tional Bank and former Maycr of this
city, died here yesterday, aged 66. He

was a lawyer, specializing in admiralty |

practice, and had lectured on admiralty
at the University of Maine. He owned
oil and lumber properties in various
parts of the United States and Canada.
He .was a. Mason and-a-~ Knight. of

IMPERIAL DIADEM VANISHES.|

Austrian Diamond and Ruby Orna-
ment Reported Missing.

A diamond and:ruby diadem, described
as part of the Imperial Austrian jewels,
disappeared two months ago from their
place of arenes. in the Spanish Con-
sulate in Vienna. Coupled with the an-
nouncement was a warning to Ameri-
cans not to buy gems represented as
part of the Austrian crown jewels.

The statement, issued on behalf of
Baron Clemens von Radowitz-Nei. who
is at the Waldorf, and Count de Korwin-
Sokolowski, who sailed for Europe last
Saturday, said in part:

“Count de Sokolowski had been a flier

with the Hungarian air. forces, and be-
cause he was intimately related to
Hungarian royalty he took unto himseif
the task of slipping out of the country
many members of the royal family
whose lives were imperiled by the revo-
lutionists. The Archduchess Blanca of
Austria, ene of the Princesses of Bour-
bon, told the Count of the royal jewels
having been secreted. The diamond-
ruhy diadem was hidden in a convent in
Vienna, and at the Archduchess’s re-
quest the Count went to Vienna when
the imperial family had been safely re-
moved to Spain, and claimed them. The
diadem was placed with the spanish
Consulate in Vienna.”’

The diadem was the property of the
Archduchess Blanca, and consists of five
stars of diamonds, with a ruby in the
centre of each star of diamonds. It is

PALO ALTO, Cal., July 20.—Edward
W. (Dad) Moulton, 74 years old, train-
er off Stanford track teams for the last
twenty years, died suddenly at his home
yesterday after a day’s illness, He is
survived by a widow and son.

Moulton was a veteran of the Indian
wars and fifty years ago had a repu-
tation in the Middle West as a runner.
He was a native of Maine.

SALTUS—John Sanford. The Salmagundi
Club announces with the deepest regret
the death of its, distinguished member,
John Sanford Saltus, which occurred in
London on the 22d of June. Since he be-
came a member of the club in 1895 he
has been an enthusiastic contributor to
the library of the club; more than half of
the five thousand and odd volumes on the
shelves, including the rare collection
of works on Louis XVII., bear his name
on the book plates. His beloved person-
ality and his generous interest in the
welfare of the organization make his
memory one of the treasures of the club.
The members of the club are requested
to attend his funeral at the Marble Col-
legiate Church, at 29th St. and 5th Av.
today at 10 A. M.

REPARATION ISSUE,

Result of Bankers’ Conference
Is Found to Be Less Nega-
tive Than It Seemed.

MADE FRENCH SEE LIGHT

Best Opportunity Since the Armi-
stice Is Opening for Germany
to. Save Herself.

By CHARLES H. GRASTY.

Copyright, 1922, by The New York Times Company.
Special Cable to THs New York TiMBEs.

LONDON, July 21.—European interest
is concentrating upon the reparations
question, The return of the Guarantee
Committee probably bringing offers from
the Wirth Government, the tentative pro-
posals for British remission of the
French debt, the favorable reception of
which in America has given them a de-
cided boost, and finally the expected
meeting of Premiers Lloyd George and
Poincaré in the near future encourage
hopes that this all important question
may be entering on ‘its final stage.

There is one essential difference be-
tween the present and past efforts. The
breaking up of the bankers’ conference

at Paris last month and the statement
of the bankers, as well as the logic of
the whole loan incident, have shaped
world sentiment toward businesslike
procedure in the reparations settlement.
It is evident that real progress has
been made in an approach to a settle-
ment. ‘Chis progress has not yet taken
visible form, but it is none the less real.
It consists largely in mental clarification
on the subject of German reparations.
Until very recently it was impossible,
in France at least, to separate
question of meting out justice to the
Germans for devastation damage and
sacrifice of life from the question of how
much could be collected from them, and
when and how. With the means at hand
in the shape of a great efficient army to
inflict, as an alternative incomparably
more terrible than any amount of in-
demnity, the partial or complete des-
truction of Germany, the Frenchman's
jaws have been set against letting the
Germans off cheaply. Why should this
people, as skillful in trade as they were
eruel in war be treated leniently by the
country -they had tried to. destroy by
force, and would later try to ruin by in-
dustrial! competition made easier for
them by this very leniency?
There has been no time

ere since the
armistice when any French

Statesman

could dare to set up against this feeling |

a program of accepting what could be
got out of Germany. It might be ra-
tional, it might be in aecordance with
ultimate self-interest, but France would
have none of it.

Effect of Bankers’ Conference.

It was the Bankers’ Conference that
turned French thought toward the un-
palatable realities. The result of the
Morgan committee’s session was in effect |

much less negative than it seemed. It}
was a friendly, even partisan committee
but, as must have been foreseen,
bound to deal with hard facts, Righteous
indignation and political spellbinding
are unaeceptable as collateral. If money |
was to be advanced, there had to be

reasonable certainty of its repayment.
When the bankers put up the shutters
and went home upon France’s refusal to |
have the subject pursued on these lines
they gave an explanation of their action
that left no room for criticism or sus-
: Here at last was a body
spoke with authority and that could not
be disposed of by hue and cry or impu-
bad motives. They had come

it w as}

| France,

BRITISH POSITION
ON FRANCE’S DEBT

‘Plain Outline’ by Government
Organ—Suggested Political
Quid Pro Quo.

Special Cable to THp New Yorn TIMES.

LONDON, Friday, July 21.—As there
is a good deal of vagueness in the minds

and

| which discussion has reached on the |
question of Setting off interallied debts |
against German reparations, The Daily
Chronicle gives the following ‘ plain
outline ’’ of the position:

‘The Prime Minister was asked in
‘Parliament last Monday about a sugges-
tion that ‘ Great Britain, while paying
her debt to America, should accept in

lieu of her debts from France, Italy and
Belgium German bonds, which would |
then be destroyed. ’ He replied that any |
such plan ‘ had the serious disadvantage |
of placing this country in a position et |
paying in full all that it had ECO ES |
from other countries during the war and

collecting nothing, either in respect of
war advances or in respect of repara-
tions.’

‘That answer,’’ The Chronicle con-
tinues, “‘is in harmony with the atti-
tude that the British Government has
hitherto consistently adopted. When Sir
Robert Horne suggested last Winter in
Paris that the French debts to Great
| Britain might be made payable in Ger-

German reparations account and help
| to reduce Germany's
payments. within
| tions, it was a condition that the United |
States should be willing in the same}
| way to accept German bonds as payment |
from us.

| The scheme was in fact to be a unt-
versal one. All allied debts to Great
| Britain and all 3ritish debts
| United States would be paid in German
| bonds, and. since the allied debts. to
| Great Britain are approximately. double
the British debt to the United States it
will be seen that the net sums taken in
| German bonds by Great Britain and the

United States—the net sacrifices accept-
ed by the two countries—would be ap-
prokfenntely equal
| ‘The present obstacle to this scheme
| lies in the altitude of American opin-
lien. The American voter burdened by
| high taxation has been told by many
of his newspapers and public men that
the way to get it down is to make the
Allies pay their debts. The only ally
who has expressed readiness and wil-
|lingness to pay is Great Britain, and
he is loath to commute this imme-
| diately available money for German
bonds whose value, if any, would be
| unrealizable till a remote date.

‘* Perhaps if he realized the relation
|of the debt question to Europe's recov-
ery and that of Europe's recovery to
America’s trade he would think other-
wise, but he does not and there are no
| substantial signs that he will. In. these
circumstances Great Britain will’ of
course adhere to her obligation to pay
her American debt. When the House
rises Sir Rebert Horne will proceed to
Washington and arrange there: with the
American Government for it to be fund-
ed over a period of years.

‘The situation as between Great Brit-
ain and France, therefore, is that the
condition upon which the British offer
was based has at present very little
|jchance of being fulfilled,. and the Brit-
|} ish Government can scarcely see its way
to go ahead without it for the reasons
so succinctly given by the Prime Min-
ister in the answer which we quoted
above.

““It is, however, conceivable . that
| France herself might give us some con-
sideration in return for our making
some set-off of the German for the
{French debt. Such consideration would
| presumably be political;. France might
| accede to our views regarding the pres-
d | ent very expensive occupation of German
territory by the allied forces.

‘“We are not aware that any definite
suggestions of this kind have ever been
made, though the idea may have been
| mooted in formal talks. At all events,
|in the critical situation now resulting
¢ som the German mark’s collapse and
j}danger to French finances, no stone of
discussion ought be left unturned.’”’

Ex-Soldiers Mourn ‘Aunt Mary’ Hall
HARRISBURG, Pa., July .20.—Gov-
ernor Sproul in a telegram today to
R. A. Dunn of Augusta, Ga,, expressed
the sorrow of Pennsylvania's. former
soldiers at the news of. the death of

Miss Mary Hall, 84 years old, known
as ‘‘ Aunt Mary ** to men of the Twen-
ty-eighth (Keystone) Division, whom
she ‘‘ mothered’? while. they were, in
camp in Georgia in 1918.

The Governor’s message was in re-
sponse to one from Dunn notifying
him of the death of Miss Hall, whom
Dunn déscribed as the “‘ only known
unreconstructed rebel.”” She also was
known as ‘‘ the Princess of the Vets’”’
and ‘‘ the Lady in Gray.’’

It’s still a little early to begin getting
out the embalming fluid for the Yan-
keesj/ This was demonstrated yesterday
at the Polo Grounds, when the corpse
gat up and moved briskly. There was
aomething reminiscent of the old and
better days in the swish of the Yankee
bats. Clean, crisp hitting, good pitch-
ing, adequate fielding—everything as it
used to be before the Hugmen decided
to lie down and become the doormat

of the American League.

The Detroit Tigers looked weak and
futile against this combination, although
even at that the Cobb team led for five

of the nine innings.
in the first inning, and this was good
until the sixth, when B. Meusel and G.
Ruth awoke and banged forth singles
that paved the way for a two-run flurry
against Red Oldham. These were runs
enough to win, as events turned out,
but Aaron Ward closed the case by driv-
ing a full-fledged home run _ into the
left-field bleachers in the eighth, with
two colleagues on the base lines. The
score was 5 to 1.

The good pitching came from blond

Carl Mays, whose: work has been so in- |

different. lately that nobody was sur-
prised when the Tigers battered him for

seven hits in the first five innings. But |

after that the Detroits got only a lone
singe and nothing came of that except
a@ little excitement before Bob Veach
closed the inning, the eighth, by flying
out to Meusel in left.
